Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: runner-up B given the same comma-ing shape as the key.

questions.question: A cinema chain's ticketing system has a standby server, but only one network technician knows the manual steps to switch over to it. What should the IT manager propose to BEST improve availability?

options.A: Give the technician an on-call phone and a spare work laptop
options.B: Add a second standby server next to the existing one
options.C: Take ticketing database backups hourly instead of nightly
options.D: Write up the failover so a second colleague can run it

questions.key_concept: A single point of failure can be a person; documented steps and a trained alternate keep failover working.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the switch-over depends on.
questions.correct_explanation: The standby server removes one single point of failure, but the one person who can use it is another. Written steps and a second trained technician mean the switch-over still works when that person is sick, away or unreachable. Making the technician easier to reach is the runner-up: it shortens delays, but service still depends on one person being available at the moment of failure.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: faster contact does help in an outage. But the service still depends on one person, who may be ill, on leave or unreachable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because spares improve availability. But a second spare needs the same manual switch-over, which still only one person can do.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because backups protect data. But backup frequency limits data loss; it does not bring service back while no one can run the switch-over.

tips: Eliminate: B adds hardware that the same single person must still switch over, and C changes how much data could be lost, not how fast service returns.
Final two: D beats A because a second trained person removes the single point of failure, while a phone only makes one person easier to reach.
Exam cue: single points of failure include people. Look for the one person, link or device everything depends on, and add a second.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.4.6 (Roles and Responsibilities: teams stay viable when members are unavailable, or alternates are designated); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR-03 (mechanisms are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Find single points of failure, such as one server, one internet link or one key person' (notes 2.2.1 Redundancy and High Availability). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and option C reworded.

questions.question: A theme park's continuity coordinator asks function owners to rate how harm grows during outages for a business impact analysis (BIA). Which outage should the BIA rate MOST severe?

options.A: Online ticket sales stop, so the year's busiest weekend loses its sales
options.B: The park news blog goes offline, so visitors miss updates
options.C: Staff payroll runs two days late, so wages reach accounts late
options.D: Ride sensor monitoring stops, so faults go unseen on running rides

questions.key_concept: A BIA rates how harm grows when each function stops; outages that put people at risk rank above financial loss.
questions.pre_read: Notice what each outage would stop, and what could follow from it.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA rates the harm each outage causes over time, and harm to people is the most severe kind. Without ride sensor monitoring, faults that could injure riders go unseen, so that function ranks above any revenue loss. Lost ticket sales on the busiest weekend is the runner-up: the money is real and grows by the hour, but it can be recovered in a way an injury cannot.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: lost sales on a peak weekend are a serious impact. But money can be recovered; a ride fault no one can see can injure people.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because visitors notice it. But a news blog outage causes little harm, even over days, and can wait behind critical functions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because every employee is affected. But a two-day pay delay is limited and recoverable, far below a risk to riders' safety.

tips: Eliminate: C is a short, recoverable delay, and B is a low-impact outage that can wait for days.
Final two: D beats A because harm to people outranks lost revenue when a BIA rates impact.
Exam cue: in any ranking of impact, people's safety comes first. Then weigh how fast harm grows for money, obligations and reputation.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Appendix B (Sample BIA Template: impact categories can include harm to individuals); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2.1 (Determine Business Processes and Recovery Criticality: MTD, RTO and RPO)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Function owners rate how harm grows at several outage lengths' (notes 2.2.3 Business Impact Analysis (BIA)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up (31 Oct 2026): option B states the rides keep running, so 'operators would stop the rides' cannot turn it into a revenue-only outage. Key letter moved from B to D (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.question: A ferry operator copies its booking database every 6 hours, against a 30-minute recovery point objective (RPO); IT proposes a hot site loaded from those same copies. What is the continuity coordinator's MOST accurate conclusion?

options.A: The hot site cuts downtime, but the copies still miss the RPO
options.B: The hot site meets the RPO, but needs a full test first
options.C: The copies meet the RPO if a restore finishes within 30 minutes
options.D: The RPO target should be reset to the 6-hour copy cycle

questions.key_concept: The RPO depends on how recent the last good copy is; a faster site shortens downtime, but data loss depends on the copies it loads.
questions.pre_read: Notice the copy schedule, the recovery target and what IT proposes.
questions.correct_explanation: The RPO looks back: with copies every 6 hours, up to 6 hours of bookings can be lost, far beyond the 30-minute limit. A hot site speeds the return to service, which helps the RTO, but it restores the same old copy. Only more frequent copies or replication close the RPO gap. The runner-up mixes the two targets: restore speed is about time, not about how much data is lost.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a hot site is the fastest recovery option and testing matters. But it loads the same 6-hour-old copies, so no test changes how much data is lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: restore speed does matter. But a fast restore meets the RTO; the RPO depends on how recent the copy is, and 6 hours is far over 30 minutes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it closes the gap. But the business sets the RPO from its needs; the coordinator reports the gap rather than bending the target to fit the copies.

tips: Eliminate: B credits a hot site with reducing data loss, and D bends the business's target to fit the current copies.
Final two: A beats C because restore speed meets the RTO; only more frequent copies or replication change how much data is lost.
Exam cue: RPO looks back to the last good copy; RTO looks forward to service returning. Sites fix time; backups and replication fix data loss.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2.1 (Determine Business Processes and Recovery Criticality: MTD, RTO and RPO); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 5.1.5 (Identification of Alternate Storage and Processing Facilities: hot sites hold the most recent backed-up data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, the business can lose; it looks back from the disruption' (notes 2.2.4 Recovery Objectives: MTD, RTO and RPO). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): pre_read no longer gives the method (rule 7); option D lost its purpose clause (rule 3); key_concept ties data loss to the copies a site loads; the hot-site citation moves from Section 3.4.3 to Section 5.1.5, which states what data a hot site holds.

questions.question: A translation agency's nightly backups go to a storage server that its domain administrator accounts can delete, and ransomware groups now target backups. Which change should the system administrator propose to BEST protect the backups?

options.A: Encrypt each backup file before writing it to storage
options.B: Run the backups every hour instead of every night
options.C: Keep one backup copy immutable for a fixed retention period
options.D: Add a nightly copy to a domain-joined server at another site

questions.key_concept: At least one backup copy should be offline or immutable, so ransomware or a stolen administrator account cannot alter or delete it.
questions.pre_read: Notice who can delete the backups today and what attackers go after.
questions.correct_explanation: Ransomware crews look for backups and use stolen administrator accounts to delete or encrypt them before striking. A copy that is immutable, or offline, cannot be changed even by an administrator account, so a clean restore stays possible. Copying to a domain-joined server at another site is the runner-up: it adds an offsite copy, as the 3-2-1 rule asks, but the same domain administrator accounts could still delete it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption keeps backups from being read. But attackers who can delete or overwrite the copies do not need to read them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more frequent copies lose less data. But every copy sits on the same deletable server, so ransomware can still wipe them all.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it adds an offsite copy, as 3-2-1 asks. But the same domain administrator accounts can delete a domain-joined server's copy, so one stolen account destroys every copy.

tips: Eliminate: A protects confidentiality when the threat is deletion, and B changes how much data could be lost, not whether the copies survive.
Final two: C beats D because an immutable copy survives a stolen administrator account; a domain-joined server at another site does not.
Exam cue: 3-2-1 is a start. Keep at least one copy offline or immutable, beyond the reach of any account an attacker could steal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-9 (System Backup); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Keep at least one copy offline or immutable, so ransomware or a stolen admin account cannot change it' (notes 2.2.5 Backups: Types, the 3-2-1 Rule and Restore Testing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): option A lost its reason clause (rule 3); stem ending reworded. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: options A and D reworded.

questions.subtopic: 2.2 Redundancy. Testing BC and DR plans
questions.question: A national lottery operator's continuity coordinator must show that its draw system really operates at the recovery site, while the main site carries on as normal. Which plan test BEST fits this goal?

options.A: A tabletop exercise where the team talks through the plan
options.B: A simulation where teams act out their recovery roles on test systems
options.C: A parallel test where the standby site runs beside production
options.D: A full interruption test where production at the main site stops

questions.key_concept: A parallel test runs systems at the recovery site while production continues; a simulation rehearses roles on test systems; a full interruption stops production.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the coordinator must prove and what must keep running.
questions.correct_explanation: A parallel test brings systems up at the recovery site and runs real work there while production carries on, so it proves the site can run the draw system. A simulation is the runner-up: it also leaves production alone and rehearses roles, but on test systems it cannot show that the recovery site itself runs the system. A full interruption would prove it, but shutting the main site is ruled out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tabletops find gaps cheaply. But talking through steps cannot prove the system actually runs at the recovery site.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it keeps production running and rehearses the team's roles. But it uses test systems, so it cannot prove the draw system actually runs at the recovery site.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is the most realistic test. But it stops the main site, which the goal rules out, and needs senior management approval because it risks a real outage.

tips: Eliminate: A is a discussion test that cannot show anything runs, and D shuts down the main site, which the goal rules out.
Final two: C beats B because a parallel test runs the real system at the recovery site beside production; a simulation rehearses on test systems.

Exam cue: choose the least disruptive test that still proves the goal. Tabletops and simulations rehearse people; a parallel test proves the real system runs at the recovery site while production carries on.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-4 (Contingency Plan Testing); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.5 (Plan Testing, Training, and Exercises)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Test in order of risk: checklist, tabletop, simulation, parallel, full interruption' (notes 2.2.7 Testing and Maintaining BC and DR Plans). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): stem no longer echoes 'runs' from the key, and the runner-up is now a simulation (B, was a checklist review), because the stem itself ruled out the full interruption test; explanations and tips follow. Key letter moved from D to C (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.question: A grocery chain's AI demand forecast drops to 79% accuracy, and its runbook, approved by the model owner, has the on-call technician start manual ordering below 85%. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.A: Report the drop and ask the model owner to approve manual ordering
options.B: Switch the stores to manual ordering, then inform the model owner
options.C: Retrain the current model on this month's data, then redeploy it
options.D: Restart the forecasting servers, then check whether accuracy recovers

questions.key_concept: When a model drifts past a set threshold, an approved runbook can give the switch to a fallback process to the practitioner on duty.
questions.pre_read: Check what the runbook says happens below the threshold, and who it names.
questions.correct_explanation: The runbook, approved by the model owner, gives the switch to manual ordering to the on-call technician once accuracy falls below 85%, and 79% is below it. So the technician acts in role: moves stores to the manual process, then tells the owner. Asking the owner to approve the switch is the runner-up: the owner does decide on retraining, but they already approved what happens below the threshold, and waiting leaves bad forecasts running.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the owner should hear about it. But they already approved manual ordering below 85% in the runbook; asking again and waiting keeps poor forecasts in use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retraining could fix drift. But retraining is the model owner's decision and takes time; the runbook calls for manual ordering now.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because restarts fix many faults. But drift means the model is losing accuracy on changed data; healthy servers still serve wrong forecasts.

tips: Eliminate: C takes over the owner's retraining decision, and D treats drift as a server fault, when the model itself is giving worse answers.
Final two: B beats A because the owner's approved runbook already gives the switch below 85% to the technician; asking again only delays it, and the owner is still told.
Exam cue: a drifting model is a continuity problem. When an approved runbook names the fallback and gives it to you, use it, then report.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 2.4 (mechanisms are in place and responsibilities assigned to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI systems that perform inconsistently with intended use); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR-03 (mechanisms are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations)

Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): option A drops the openly passive 'then wait' and now starts 'Report', so neither opening word predicts the key; the stem no longer repeats the key's wording. Fix-up (31 Oct 2026): option B says 'the stores', not 'all stores', which the stem never states.

questions.question: A newspaper's AI threat-monitoring tool keeps its tuned detection rules, settings and logs only on the servers it watches. What should the security analyst propose to BEST keep detection working through a ransomware recovery?

options.A: Mirror rules, settings and logs to a server on the same network
options.B: Copy rules, settings and logs to separate offline storage
options.C: Pause monitoring until the server restores are finished
options.D: Retrain the tool on fresh traffic once the servers are restored

questions.key_concept: Detection tools need their rules, settings and logs backed up away from the systems they watch, so monitoring survives the event.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the tool's knowledge lives and what ransomware would reach.
questions.correct_explanation: Ransomware that encrypts the watched servers would take the tool's tuned rules, settings and logs with them, leaving recovery unwatched. Copies kept away from those servers can be restored early, so detection works while systems come back. A mirror on a server in the same network is the runner-up: it keeps a second copy, but the same attack can reach both.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a mirror keeps a second copy. But a server on the same network can be encrypted in the same attack, taking the copy with it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because recovery is busy. But attackers exploit the confusion, and restored systems need watching; monitoring belongs early in recovery.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the tool can learn again. But retraining takes time and loses months of tuning, leaving recovery poorly watched.

tips: Eliminate: C drops monitoring just when attackers exploit the confusion, and D loses months of tuning and leaves a blind period while the tool relearns.
Final two: B beats A because copies on separate offline storage survive the attack; a mirror on the same network can be encrypted at the same time.
Exam cue: detection must survive the outage it warns about. Keep its rules, settings and logs apart from the systems it watches.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-9(3) (System Backup | Separate Storage for Critical Information); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-9(2) (Protection of Audit Information | Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Back up detection rules, settings and logs away from the monitored systems' (notes 2.2.9 AI-Assisted Detection and Resilience). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): stem no longer echoes cc_d2_030's 'restore monitoring early' (the lesson is where the copy is kept); option B lost its reason clause (rule 3). Fix-up (31 Oct 2026): key and runner-up both carry the stem's rules, settings and logs, so they differ only in where the copy is kept (rule 10). Key letter moved from C to B (31 Oct 2026) to break a periodic key order; options and letter references swapped, text unchanged.

questions.question: A game studio employee reports a lost work phone two days late, saying they did not know who to tell or whether it counted. Which change should the security manager propose to BEST improve reporting?

options.A: Publish one simple reporting route with examples of what to report
options.B: Formally warn the employee for reporting the loss two days late
options.C: Add a module on looking after devices to each employee's yearly course
options.D: Turn on remote wipe and tracking for every work phone

questions.key_concept: Reporting must be easy: one clear route and plain examples of what counts get incidents reported fast.
questions.pre_read: Notice why the report came late and what the manager wants to improve.
questions.correct_explanation: The delay came from not knowing where or what to report, and every hour a lost device goes unreported is time to misuse it. One simple route, with examples such as lost devices, wrong sends and odd messages, removes that doubt for everyone. A device-care module is the runner-up: it may cut losses, but the question asks about reporting, and care training does not tell staff where to report.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the delay did add risk. But punishing a reporter teaches everyone to hide mistakes, making future reports slower, or absent.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it targets the loss itself. But the delay came from not knowing the route, not from careless handling.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because remote wipe limits harm from a lost phone. But it works only once someone reports the loss, and does nothing about why the report came late.

tips: Eliminate: B punishes the reporting the studio needs more of, and D adds a technical control that still waits on a report.
Final two: A beats C because the delay came from not knowing where to report; device training targets the loss, not the reporting.
Exam cue: fix the cause the stem names. If people report late because the route is unclear, make reporting simple and give examples.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving); NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 (Building a Cybersecurity and Privacy Learning Program)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Reporting is easy and safe, with thanks instead of blame for honest mistakes', using the 'easy' half (notes 2.3.1 Security Culture and Leadership). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and options C, D reworded. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded with 'with' instead of a comma-ing tail.

questions.question: A city transit agency's awareness lead learns that a fake parcel-delivery text is targeting staff phones this week; the yearly course runs in six months. Which step is BEST for reaching all staff?

options.A: Rerun the full yearly security course for all staff this month
options.B: Alert all staff with a picture of the fake text
options.C: Give the help desk team role-based training on the parcel scam
options.D: Ask staff to forward the fake text to coworkers as a warning

questions.key_concept: Awareness reaches everyone with short, timely messages about current threats; training builds job skills for particular roles.
questions.pre_read: Notice who is targeted and how soon they need to know.
questions.correct_explanation: Awareness activities run all year and respond to current threats with short, timely messages for everyone. A brief alert now, showing what the text looks like and how to report it, reaches all staff while the scam is live. Rerunning the full course is the runner-up: it reaches everyone too, but it is slow and heavy for one new scam, and training time is better aimed at specific roles.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it does reach every employee. But a full course is slow to organize and heavy for one live scam; a quick alert does the job this week.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because role-based training builds skills. But this text targets every employee's phone, so training one team leaves everyone else unwarned.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it spreads the warning. But forwarding passes on the live lure and its link; warnings should come from the awareness lead.

tips: Eliminate: C trains one team for a scam aimed at everyone, and D spreads the live lure instead of a safe warning.
Final two: B beats A because awareness is short and timely for everyone; a full course is too slow and heavy for one live scam.
Exam cue: awareness is short, frequent and for everyone; training builds skills for particular roles. A new threat hitting everyone now calls for awareness.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 Section 2.7.1 (Awareness Activities: ongoing, timely messages for all users throughout the year); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(6) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Cyber Threat Environment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Awareness reaches everyone through short, frequent messages, such as reminders and brief campaigns' (notes 2.3.2 Awareness, Training and Education). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: blind-tester flag: key reworded for clarity ('with a picture of the fake text').

questions.question: A mining company's security analyst sees that its chief financial officer received an email built from details of their conference talk, asking for a rushed payment. Which term names this attack MOST precisely?

options.A: A smishing attack
options.B: A vishing attack
options.C: A spear phishing attack
options.D: A whaling attack

questions.key_concept: Whaling is spear phishing aimed at senior executives, often seeking payments or sensitive data and built from public details about them.
questions.pre_read: Notice every detail given about the message and the person who received it.
questions.correct_explanation: Whaling is spear phishing aimed at a senior executive, the 'big fish', often asking for payments or sensitive data and built from public details about the target. A chief financial officer targeted with details from their own talk fits exactly. Spear phishing is the runner-up: it is also tailored to one person, but whaling is the more precise name when the target is a top executive.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because smishing is a phishing variant. But smishing arrives by text message, and this lure came by email.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vishing also targets individuals. But vishing uses voice calls, and this attack was an email.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the email is tailored to one person. But when that person is a senior executive, whaling is the more precise term.

tips: Eliminate: A and B name the wrong channel, text message and voice call, for a lure that came by email.
Final two: D beats C because whaling is spear phishing aimed at a senior executive, so it names this attack more precisely.
Exam cue: when two terms fit, pick the narrowest the facts support. All whaling is spear phishing; a senior executive target makes whaling the precise name.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Whaling: spear phishing aimed at senior executives or other high-value people' (notes 2.3.4 Phishing and Its Variants, types table). Superset runner-up kept on purpose: the stem asks for the most precise term. Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up (31 Oct 2026): Exam cue teaches choosing the narrower fitting term, not cc_d2_036's channel-versus-target naming; pre_read no longer hands over the method.

questions.question: A furniture maker's IT manager is preparing a monthly security report for managers. Under NIST SP 800-55 definitions, which item is MOST accurately a metric rather than a raw measure?

options.A: 1,850 of 2,000 staff accounts have multifactor sign-in turned on
options.B: 340 suspicious emails were reported by staff this month
options.C: Accounts with multifactor sign-in: 1,850, against a 1,960 target
options.D: Share of staff accounts with multifactor sign-in this month: 92.5%

questions.key_concept: A measure is a raw, quantified value; a metric compares measures with a set target to track progress and support decisions.
questions.pre_read: Think about what each item would let managers decide.
questions.correct_explanation: Under NIST SP 800-55, a measure is a quantifiable value from measurement, such as a count or a share of accounts. A metric tracks progress with respect to a set target, so the count shown against its 1,960 target tells managers how far they are from the goal. The bare percentage is the runner-up: it looks calculated, but with no target beside it, it cannot say whether 92.5% is good enough.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is precise. But it is a single raw count; with no target, nobody can tell whether 1,850 is good or bad.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reports show staff are alert. But it is a single raw count with no target, so managers cannot tell whether 340 is good or bad.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a percentage looks like a finished metric. But 92.5% only restates 1,850 of 2,000; with no target beside it, it is still a measure.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are single raw counts, of accounts and of reported emails, with no goal to judge either against.
Final two: C beats D because it sets the count against a 1,960 target; a percentage with no target is still a measure, however calculated it looks.
Exam cue: a measure is a raw number; a metric sets it against a target so it can drive a decision. Look for the target.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 1.4 (Document Terminology: measures are quantifiable values and metrics track progress with respect to a set target)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Compare each result with a baseline and a target' (notes 2.4.1 Measures and Metrics: The Basics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Fix-up (31 Oct 2026): stem names NIST SP 800-55 because older usage calls any ratio a metric; the key now sets a count against a target, so the runner-up is no longer a subset of the key. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): 'IT lead' became 'IT manager' (canonical role names).

questions.question: A concert promoter's security manager must show the board what ransomware outages mean for the business. Which measure BEST fits this audience?

options.A: Revenue lost for each hour that ticket sales are offline
options.B: Average hours taken to restore the ticketing system
options.C: Share of servers with endpoint protection installed
options.D: Number of malware alerts the tools raised this quarter

questions.key_concept: Impact measures express security results in business terms, such as lost revenue, and suit boards and executives.
questions.pre_read: Notice who the audience is and what they decide.
questions.correct_explanation: Boards decide on money, mission and risk, so they need impact measures that turn security results into business terms. Revenue lost per hour of ticket-sales outage tells them directly what ransomware costs. Average restore time is the runner-up: it is a useful efficiency measure, but the board would still have to translate hours into business harm themselves.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: restore time matters and links to impact. But it is an efficiency measure for operators; the board needs the business cost those hours create.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because coverage shows a control exists. But it is an implementation measure and says nothing about what outages cost the business.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it shows activity. But an alert count reflects tool volume, not business effect, and means little to a board.

tips: Eliminate: C shows only that a control is installed, and D counts tool activity; neither says what outages cost.
Final two: A beats B because the board needs the business effect; restore time is an efficiency measure that still needs translating.
Exam cue: match the measure to the audience. Boards and executives want impact in business terms; operators want implementation and efficiency measures.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.3 (Types of Measures: implementation, effectiveness, efficiency and impact)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Executives need impact measures; operators need implementation and efficiency measures' (notes 2.4.2 Types of Security Measures). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.question: A wind farm operator's draft quarterly report, owned by the security manager, shows 86% of servers patched, but the dashboard shows 91% for the same month. What should the reviewing analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Change the report to 91%, then tell the security manager
options.B: Release the report on schedule with the draft 86% figure
options.C: Drop the patching figure from this quarter's report
options.D: Flag both figures and their sources to the security manager

questions.key_concept: The same metric must show the same value in every view; a mismatch goes to the report's owner before release.
questions.pre_read: Notice who owns the report and what is still unknown about the two figures.
questions.correct_explanation: The same metric must show the same value in every view, so a gap between report and dashboard means a definition, query or cutoff differs. The analyst flags both figures and their sources to the security manager, who owns the report, before it goes out. Changing the report to 91% is the runner-up: it makes the views agree, but the dashboard might be the wrong one, and the report is not the analyst's to change.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the views must match. But nobody yet knows which figure is right, and the report belongs to the security manager, so the analyst flags it first.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the report is due and the gap looks small. But leaders compare views, and an unexplained gap erodes trust in every number reported.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it avoids publishing a number that may be wrong. But it keeps the gap from leaders; the owner must learn the views disagree so the cause gets fixed.

tips: Eliminate: B releases numbers that disagree, and C drops a figure leaders rely on instead of tracing why the views differ.
Final two: D beats A because the cause is unknown and the report is the security manager's; flag both sources rather than picking one.
Exam cue: one metric, one value in every view. When views disagree, trace the sources and tell the owner before release.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.2 (Characteristics of Measures: consistency, time-based reference and replicability); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OV-03 (organizational cybersecurity risk management performance is evaluated and reviewed for adjustments needed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Show trends, not single snapshots, and use the same definitions in every view' (notes 2.4.5 Dashboards, Scorecards and Reports). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): option B lost its reason clause (rule 3); its explanation names the new temptation. Option A keeps 'act, then tell the owner' because cc_d2_047 A no longer uses that wording and cc_d2_057's key does, so the form predicts nothing. Fix-up (31 Oct 2026): key and option B lengths brought into one band so length no longer points to the key.

questions.subtopic: 2.4 Measuring effectiveness. Using measurement to improve
questions.question: A stadium's monthly security report has 45 metrics; leaders used just 8 for decisions last year, and none of the rest is mandatory or an early warning. What should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Keep reporting the 45 metrics with their full history
options.B: Retire the 37 unused metrics and archive their past data
options.C: Add a one-page summary above the existing 45 metrics
options.D: Replace the current set with five new metrics chosen from scratch

questions.key_concept: Metrics that drive no decision should be retired deliberately, keeping their history, so effort goes to the ones that matter.
questions.pre_read: Notice how many metrics leaders actually use.
questions.correct_explanation: Metrics exist to drive decisions; ones nobody uses cost effort to collect and bury the eight that matter. Retiring them deliberately, with leaders' agreement and their history kept, makes the report sharper and frees effort for new risks. A summary page on top is the runner-up: it helps readers, but all 45 still have to be collected, checked and explained every month.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because history matters. But history can be kept while collection stops; keeping unused metrics live wastes effort and hides what matters.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a summary does help leaders. But all 45 metrics still have to be gathered and checked each month, and the clutter remains.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it starts fresh. But it drops the eight metrics leaders actually use and breaks every trend they rely on.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps unused metrics running for completeness, and D throws out the eight metrics leaders actually use.
Final two: B beats C because retiring unused metrics removes the work and the clutter; a summary page only hides it.
Exam cue: a metric that drives no decision is a candidate to retire. Retire on purpose and keep the history; never keep or delete metrics by habit.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OV-03 (organizational cybersecurity risk management performance is evaluated and reviewed for adjustments needed); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.2 (Developing, Testing, and Validating Measures: organizations cannot take infinite measures, so measures follow stated priorities)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Retire metrics no one uses, and add ones for new risks such as artificial intelligence (AI) use' (notes 2.4.6 Using Measurement to Improve). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Final pass (31 Oct 2026): stem states that none of the unused metrics is required or used as an early warning, so retiring them is the single best answer. Option A lost its reason clause (rule 3). Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): 'metrics analyst' became 'security analyst' (canonical role names).

questions.question: An e-scooter rental firm's chief executive asks the security analyst how to tell whether its new governance, risk and compliance (GRC) program is working. Which sign is BEST?

options.A: Named owners now tie every security decision to the business goals
options.B: The firm passes every compliance assessment it schedules this year
options.C: Policies and risks now sit in one purchased GRC platform
options.D: Each team keeps its own risk list in its preferred format

questions.key_concept: GRC works when security decisions serve business goals with clear owners; passed audits or a new platform alone do not show that.
questions.pre_read: Recall the three parts of GRC and what joins them.
questions.correct_explanation: GRC joins governance, risk management and compliance so security work serves business goals, with clear accountability and one shared view of risk. Named owners tying each decision to a goal show that joining at work. Passing every compliance assessment is the runner-up: it shows set obligations were met, but compliance is only one part, and risks outside those rules can still go unmanaged.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: compliance is one part of GRC. But passing assessments proves only that set obligations were met, not that risks are managed or that security serves business goals.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because GRC platforms are common. But a tool only stores records; without owners and decisions behind them, a platform changes nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because teams know their own risks best. But separate lists in different formats are the silos GRC replaces with one shared view of risk.

tips: Eliminate: C treats GRC as software to buy, and D keeps the separate team risk lists GRC is meant to join.
Final two: A beats B because compliance is one part of GRC; the program works when security choices follow business goals with clear owners.
Exam cue: judge GRC by alignment and accountability, not by audit results or tools alone.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-01 (the organizational mission is understood and informs cybersecurity risk management); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'GRC exists so security serves business goals. Its value is alignment, clear accountability and one shared view of risk, not any single tool' (notes 2.1.1 GRC Purpose and Importance). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded.

questions.question: In a bus tour operator's encryption rollout RACI chart, IT staff do the work, the security manager answers for the result, and department heads agree team dates beforehand. Which role BEST fits the heads?

options.A: Responsible for the rollout
options.B: Accountable for the rollout
options.C: Consulted on the rollout
options.D: Informed of the rollout

questions.key_concept: In a RACI chart, Consulted people give input before the work, Informed people are told the outcome, and only one person is Accountable.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the department heads do, and when.
questions.correct_explanation: Consulted people give input before or during the work, and here the heads must agree each team's date before work begins. Informed is the runner-up: the heads will hear how the rollout went, but Informed people are told after the fact and have no say beforehand. The security manager already answers for the result, and a task has exactly one Accountable person.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the heads' teams are affected. But Responsible means doing the work, and IT staff do it here; the heads only agree their team's date beforehand.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because agreeing a date sounds like sign-off. But the security manager already answers for the result, and a task has exactly one Accountable person.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the heads will be told how the rollout went. But Informed people hear the outcome afterward; these heads must give input before work begins.

tips: Eliminate: A belongs to the IT staff who do the work, and B already belongs to the security manager, since each task has exactly one.
Final two: C beats D because the heads give input before work begins; Informed people only hear the outcome afterward.
Exam cue: in RACI, input before the work means Consulted, news after it means Informed, and only one person is Accountable.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A RACI chart (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) maps each task to people' (notes 2.1.3 GRC Accountability: RACI and Reporting Lines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A fence builder's payment processor contract requires monthly firewall reviews, owned by the network manager; the security analyst, who logs findings by procedure, sees 2 of 12 months unrecorded. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Record the control as met for the year, with no finding
options.B: Record a finding with a due date for the network manager
options.C: Write up the two missing reviews from the team's memory
options.D: Ask the network manager to run the two missed reviews

questions.key_concept: A compliance gap becomes a recorded finding with an owner and a due date; late or rebuilt records cannot prove past months.
questions.pre_read: Notice who owns the reviews and who logs findings.
questions.correct_explanation: Evidence is created as the work happens, so two unrecorded months are a gap that later effort cannot fill. The procedure gives the analyst the job of logging findings, so they record one, with the network manager as owner and a due date. Asking the manager to run the two missed reviews is the runner-up: it restarts the control, but late reviews cannot prove those months, and the gap stays unrecorded.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because most reviews have records. But two monthly reviews have no evidence, and recording the control as met overstates compliance.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it fills the record. But a review written up later from memory is not evidence it happened, and it misleads anyone who relies on it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the reviews must restart. But reviews run now cannot prove the missed months, and the procedure has the analyst log the gap as a finding first.

tips: Eliminate: A counts a control with two unproven months as met, and C creates records after the fact, which proves nothing.
Final two: B beats D because late reviews cannot cover past months; the procedure has the analyst record the gap as a finding with an owner.
Exam cue: when evidence is missing, record the gap as a finding with an owner and a due date; never backfill or round up.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2 (Control Assessments)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Check on a schedule, and track each gap as a finding with an owner and due date' (notes 2.1.4 Compliance Obligations and Evidence). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: role 'compliance analyst' became 'security analyst'.

questions.question: A cosmetics maker's main retail partner requires suppliers to report progress against the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, and senior management will choose the firm's framework. Which option should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: The framework the IT manager used at a previous employer
options.B: The framework listing the most separate controls
options.C: NIST CSF 2.0 with its current and target profiles
options.D: ISO/IEC 27001 certification, with a CSF 2.0 mapping later

questions.key_concept: Choose a framework by what leaders, customers or contracts ask to see; habit, size or a certificate nobody asked for are weaker reasons.
questions.pre_read: Notice who is asking to see what.
questions.correct_explanation: Frameworks are chosen by need: start from what leaders, customers or contracts ask to see. The main retail partner wants supplier progress reported against CSF 2.0, and its current and target profiles show exactly that progress. ISO/IEC 27001 certification with a later CSF 2.0 mapping is the runner-up: it is respected, but no one here asked for a certificate, and the firm would run a second framework just to report against the one required.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because familiarity speeds the work. But one person's past experience is not a business need; the partner's requirement should drive the choice.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more controls feel safer. But a framework's size says nothing about fit, and a long list the firm cannot run wastes effort.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: ISO/IEC 27001 is respected and certifiable. But nobody asked for a certificate, and the partner wants CSF 2.0 progress reported directly, not through a later mapping.

tips: Eliminate: A picks by one person's habit, and B picks by size; neither starts from what the business must show.
Final two: C beats D because the partner requires CSF 2.0 progress; a certificate nobody requested, mapped across later, adds work and delays that report.
Exam cue: pick frameworks by who needs to see what; let leaders, customers and contracts drive the choice.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed); NIST CSF 2.0 Section 3.1 (CSF Profiles: Organizational Profiles are used to understand, tailor, assess, prioritize and communicate outcomes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Start from what leaders, customers or contracts ask to see' (notes 2.1.5 Choosing and Mapping Frameworks in GRC). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): 'IT lead' became 'IT manager' (canonical role names). Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded with 'with' instead of a comma-ing tail.

questions.question: A freight rail company's new governance, risk and compliance (GRC) platform pulls settings from its systems each night and flags any that drift. Which task MOST clearly still needs a person?

options.A: Deciding how to respond when a control check fails
options.B: Gathering each server's patch level on a set schedule
options.C: Flagging a firewall setting that changed overnight
options.D: Recording which policy version each employee acknowledged

questions.key_concept: GRC platforms automate collecting, flagging and record-keeping; deciding what to do about a failed control stays with its owner.
questions.pre_read: Sort each task into routine record-keeping or a judgment call.
questions.correct_explanation: GRC platforms automate routine work: collecting settings on a schedule, flagging drift and keeping policy versions and acknowledgments. Deciding how to respond to a failed control is a judgment, so it stays with the control or risk owner. Recording acknowledged policy versions is the runner-up: it feels like admin a person must do, but tracking versions and acknowledgments is exactly what a policy module does.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because patch data matters. But collecting settings on a schedule is the core of automated evidence gathering.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an overnight change sounds urgent. But flagging drift from approved settings is what automated collection does.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: someone must keep acknowledgment records. But policy management tracks versions and acknowledgments automatically; no judgment is needed.

tips: Eliminate: B and C are scheduled collection and drift flagging, the routine work GRC automation exists to do.
Final two: A beats D because recording acknowledgments is routine record-keeping a policy module handles, while responding to a failure needs an owner's judgment.
Exam cue: tools collect, flag and record; people decide, especially about risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Tools collect and display data. People still decide risk treatment, approve policies and fix gaps' (notes 2.1.6 GRC Tools and Automation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A concert hall's risk register links patron data exposure, owned by the operations director, to an encryption control that failed today's test. How should the analyst who updates the register BEST record and report this?

options.A: Mark the risk accepted until the control passes a retest
options.B: Remove the failed control's link from the register entry
options.C: Note the failure in the test log, then tell the director
options.D: Mark the control failed in the entry, then tell the director

questions.key_concept: A failed linked control changes the risk's register status at once, and the owner decides the response; a note kept elsewhere is not enough.
questions.pre_read: Ask where someone checking this risk would look first.
questions.correct_explanation: Each register entry links to the controls that treat the risk, so when one fails the risk has lost a treatment. Marking the control failed in the entry shows that at once, and telling the operations director lets them decide the response. Noting the failure in the test log, then telling the director, is the runner-up: the owner hears of it, but anyone reading the register still sees the risk as fully treated.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a retest is coming. But accepting risk belongs to the risk owner within tolerance, or senior management beyond it, never to the analyst.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a failed control seems not to count. But removing the link hides that the risk lost a control, so the entry looks healthier than it is.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the director hears of it and the test log records it. But the register still shows the control working, so readers overrate how well the risk is treated.

tips: Eliminate: A has the analyst accept risk, which only the risk owner or senior management may do, and B removes evidence that the risk lost a control.
Final two: D beats C because the register is where the risk's status lives; telling the director while only the test log changes leaves the entry out of date.
Exam cue: when a linked control fails, update the risk's entry at once and let the owner decide the response.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Each entry links to the controls that treat the risk, so a failed control changes its status' (notes 2.1.7 Tolerances and the Risk Register in GRC). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A burst pipe floods a carpet maker's basement server room while its lights are still on, and a coworker heads downstairs to rescue the file server. What should the system administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Stop the coworker and keep everyone out of the flooded room
options.B: Go down with the coworker and lift the server above the water
options.C: Shut the server down remotely, then carry it out of the room
options.D: Restore the server's offsite backup at the recovery site

questions.key_concept: Switching off a server does not make a flooded room safe: keep people out until the room's power is cut and it is declared safe.
questions.pre_read: Picture the room and the people near it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standing water with the room's power still on can electrocute anyone who enters, and a coworker is heading into it. The administrator stops them and keeps everyone out until the building's power is cut and the room is declared safe. Shutting the server down remotely is the runner-up: it feels like making the room safe, but it stops one machine, not the room's power, so the water stays live.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because two people feel safer than one. But live power in standing water can kill anyone who enters, and no server is worth that risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a remote shutdown feels like making the room safe. But it stops one server, not the room's power, so carrying it out still puts people in live water.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because restoring from the offsite copy is the right recovery step. But it does nothing for the coworker heading into live water, who must be stopped first.

tips: Eliminate: B sends people into live water, and D starts recovery while a coworker is still heading into danger.
Final two: A beats C because a remote shutdown stops the server, not the room's power; people stay out until the room is made safe.
Exam cue: a hazard is safe only once its source is made safe, such as the room's power being cut; switching off one device does not do that.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 2.2.8 (Occupant Emergency Plan (OEP)); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 2.2 (Types of Plans: Business Continuity Plan and Disaster Recovery Plan)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Human safety comes first: account for people before saving equipment or data' (notes 2.2.2 Business Continuity vs Disaster Recovery). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A glassworks' continuity coordinator is starting a business impact analysis (BIA), and a colleague suggests first rating how likely floods, fires and cyberattacks are. Which approach should the coordinator propose as BEST?

options.A: List the servers and rate how critical each one is
options.B: Rate likelihood first, then study just the likely events
options.C: Score each function on likelihood and impact together
options.D: Rate each function's impact at several outage lengths

questions.key_concept: A BIA measures impact over time for each business function and leaves likelihood to the separate risk assessment.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a BIA starts from and what it measures.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA asks how bad it gets, over time, if each business function stops, so owners rate impact at several outage lengths. Likelihood belongs to the risk assessment. Scoring likelihood and impact together is the runner-up: it is a sound risk assessment method, but blending in likelihood would rank a rare but crippling outage too low for recovery planning.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because systems are easy to list. But a BIA starts from business functions; servers matter only because functions depend on them, alongside people and suppliers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it saves effort. But a BIA measures impact, not likelihood, and skipping unlikely events leaves the worst outages unplanned.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: likelihood and impact together are a real risk method. But that is the risk assessment; a BIA measures impact over time so recovery targets can be set.

tips: Eliminate: A starts from servers instead of business functions, and B lets likelihood decide what the BIA studies.
Final two: D beats C because a BIA measures impact over time; likelihood belongs to the separate risk assessment.
Exam cue: a BIA means impact over time for each function; a risk assessment adds likelihood.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2.1 (Determine Business Processes and Recovery Criticality: MTD, RTO and RPO); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The BIA measures impact over time. Likelihood belongs to the risk assessment' (notes 2.2.3 Business Impact Analysis (BIA)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: Two vineyards in one river valley plan a reciprocal agreement to host each other's order systems after a disaster, instead of a warm site. Which weakness should the security analyst flag as MOST important?

options.A: The agreement will cost more each year than a warm site
options.B: Each vineyard's staff could see the other's customer data
options.C: Reciprocal sites hold no equipment, like a cold site
options.D: A single regional hazard could shut down both sites at once

questions.key_concept: A recovery site must sit outside the hazards that could hit the main site; a nearby partner can fail in the same event.
questions.pre_read: Consider how each weakness would play out on the day of a disaster.
questions.correct_explanation: A recovery site must be far enough away that one regional hazard cannot hit both sites. Two vineyards in one valley share floods, fires and power cuts, so the event that closes one could close the other, leaving no recovery at all. Data exposure is the runner-up: partners could see each other's records, but access rules and separation can manage that; a shared hazard cannot be managed away.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because any agreement has costs. But reciprocal agreements are among the cheapest options; their weakness is reliability, not price.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: data exposure is a real concern at a shared site. But access rules and separation can manage it; a shared regional hazard leaves no site to recover to.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because no space is rented. But each partner runs real equipment at its own site; the question is whether that site survives the same event.

tips: Eliminate: A gets the cost wrong, since reciprocal deals are cheap, and C confuses a partner's working site with an empty cold site.
Final two: D beats B because data exposure is a real but manageable weakness, controlled by access rules; a site hit by the same disaster gives no recovery at all.
Exam cue: a recovery site in the same hazard zone is no recovery site; check distance before cost or convenience.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.4.3 (Alternate Sites); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-7(1) (Alternate Processing Site | Separation from Primary Site)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Keep it far enough away that one regional event, such as a flood, cannot hit both sites' (notes 2.2.6 Recovery Sites). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded.

questions.subtopic: 2.2 Redundancy. Testing BC and DR plans
questions.question: A seed company's continuity coordinator has each team lead read their section of the recovery plan and confirm its contacts and steps are current, with no meeting. Which test is this MOST accurately?

options.A: A checklist test of the plan's contents
options.B: A tabletop exercise walking through a scenario
options.C: A parallel test run at the recovery site
options.D: A simulation with staff acting out their roles

questions.key_concept: A checklist test has each person review their part of the plan for accuracy; a tabletop gathers the team to talk through a scenario.
questions.pre_read: Recall the plan tests from least to most disruptive.
questions.correct_explanation: A checklist test, the lightest kind, has each person review their part of the plan and confirm contacts, steps and supplies are current. A tabletop exercise is the runner-up: it is also low risk and discussion-based, but it brings the team together to talk through a scenario, and here no one meets. Parallel and simulation tests run systems or have staff act out roles.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a tabletop is also low risk and touches no systems. But it gathers the team to discuss a scenario together, and these leads work alone.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it checks the recovery site. But a parallel test runs systems at that site beside production; reading plan sections runs nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because staff check their own roles. But a simulation has them act out a scenario in real time; here they only read and confirm.

tips: Eliminate: C runs systems at the recovery site, and D has staff act out a scenario; this test only reads the plan.
Final two: A beats B because each lead reviews their section alone; a tabletop brings the team together to discuss a scenario.
Exam cue: reading and checking the plan is a checklist test, talking it through together is a tabletop, and acting it out is a simulation.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-4 (Contingency Plan Testing); NIST SP 800-84 Section 4 (Tabletop Exercises: discussion-based events)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Test in order of risk: checklist, tabletop, simulation, parallel, full interruption' (notes 2.2.7 Testing and Maintaining BC and DR Plans). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A dental lab's client chatbot runs on an outside provider's AI model, and its recovery plan covers only the lab's own servers. Which addition should the continuity coordinator propose as BEST?

options.A: More frequent backups of the lab's own web servers
options.B: A fallback way to answer clients if the AI vendor fails
options.C: Versioned backups of the chatbot's prompts and settings
options.D: An alert that fires when the provider's model slows or stops

questions.key_concept: When an AI service depends on an outside provider, the recovery plan needs a fallback for the provider's outage, not just backups of local parts.
questions.pre_read: List what the chatbot needs in order to work.
questions.correct_explanation: The chatbot needs the provider's model, which the lab cannot restore from its own backups. A fallback, such as a staffed queue or a simple answer page, keeps clients served when the AI vendor fails. Versioned backups of prompts and settings are the runner-up: they help rebuild the chatbot, but they cannot run it while the provider's model is unavailable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because backups support recovery. But the lab's servers are not the weak point; the chatbot stops whenever the provider's model is unreachable.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: prompts and settings should be backed up and versioned. But they need the provider's model to run, so they cannot keep clients served during its outage.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fast detection matters. But an alert only reports the provider's outage; clients still go unserved until a fallback exists.

tips: Eliminate: A backs up servers that are not the weak point, and D detects the outage without keeping clients served.
Final two: B beats C because backups of prompts and settings still need the provider's model; only a fallback works while it is down.
Exam cue: for any outside service a function depends on, plan what happens when that service is unavailable.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 3.1 (AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored, and risk controls are applied and documented); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-2 (Contingency Plan)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Plan a fallback, such as an earlier model version or a manual process' (notes 2.2.8 Backing Up AI Systems and Model Drift). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key says 'AI vendor' instead of 'provider' so 'vendor' is not only on distractors; explanation matched.

questions.question: An art supply wholesaler's awareness lead must tell leaders whether a year-long security culture program is working. Which sign is BEST?

options.A: Every employee finished and passed this year's awareness course
options.B: Most staff rated security as important in the yearly survey
options.C: The security team grew from two people to five
options.D: Staff report their own mistakes quickly, without being asked

questions.key_concept: Culture shows in what people do unprompted, such as reporting their own mistakes; completions, survey answers and team size show less.
questions.pre_read: Compare what each sign actually shows about staff.
questions.correct_explanation: Security culture is the habits people show when no one is checking, and choosing to report one's own mistake quickly is exactly that behavior. Survey ratings are the runner-up: they capture attitudes and can help, but people may say security matters without acting on it. Course completion shows attendance, and a bigger security team shows investment, not staff habits.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because completion is easy to measure. But finishing a course shows attendance, not whether anyone behaves differently afterward.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: surveys do capture attitudes. But saying security matters is not the same as acting on it; unprompted reporting shows the habit itself.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more staff means more effort. But culture belongs to everyone; a larger security team says nothing about how other staff behave.

tips: Eliminate: A measures attendance, and C measures the security team's size; neither shows how staff act.
Final two: D beats B because survey answers report attitudes, while self-reported mistakes show what staff actually do.
Exam cue: judge culture by behavior, especially reporting, rather than by completions, surveys or headcount.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving); NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 (Building a Cybersecurity and Privacy Learning Program)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Culture is judged by behavior, such as reporting rates, not course completion' (notes 2.3.1 Security Culture and Leadership). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and options A, C reworded.

questions.question: A national rowing federation's help desk technician wants to move into a security analyst career over the next few years, and the federation will fund one option. Which learning fits this goal BEST?

options.A: The yearly awareness course for every employee, taken again
options.B: A part-time degree program in information security
options.C: Role-based training on the help desk's current security duties
options.D: Monthly security reminders sent to every employee

questions.key_concept: Education, such as a degree, builds the deep understanding a security career needs; training targets a current role and awareness reaches everyone.
questions.pre_read: Notice whose goal this is and how long it spans.
questions.correct_explanation: The technician's goal is a future career, which calls for education: long programs, such as degrees, that build deep understanding over months or years. Role-based training on help desk duties is the runner-up: it is valuable and job-specific, but it sharpens the current role rather than preparing for a new one. Awareness courses and reminders keep everyone alert, not career-ready.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because repetition reinforces basics. But the all-staff course is awareness for everyone; repeating it builds no deeper knowledge for a new career.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: role-based training builds real skills. But it targets the technician's current help desk duties, not the deeper knowledge a security analyst career needs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because regular reminders keep security in mind. But brief messages are awareness for all staff and build no career-level understanding.

tips: Eliminate: A and D are awareness for all staff, which keeps security in mind but builds no deep knowledge.
Final two: B beats C because role-based training sharpens the current job; a career change needs education's deeper, longer learning.
Exam cue: awareness for everyone, training for a role's tasks, education for a career; match the option to the learner's goal.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 10.2 (Awareness and Training: raising awareness, building job skills and building in-depth knowledge)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Awareness keeps security in mind for everyone, training builds job-specific skills for particular roles, and education builds deeper understanding for those whose careers need it' (notes 2.3.2 Awareness, Training and Education). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026. Blind re-test fix (4 Nov 2026): key reworded so it is not the only 'category, such as example' option.

questions.question: An employee at a tile manufacturer finds a memory stick labeled 'Holiday party photos' on the floor of the staff parking lot. What is the employee's BEST action?

options.A: Plug it into a work computer to find its owner
options.B: Throw it in the trash so nobody else can use it
options.C: Drop it, unplugged, in the lost-and-found box at reception
options.D: Hand it to the security team without plugging it in

questions.key_concept: A found memory stick may be baiting; hand it unplugged to the security team, who can examine it safely and warn others.
questions.pre_read: Think about why someone might leave a labeled memory stick where staff will find it.
questions.correct_explanation: A labeled stick left where staff will find it is a classic baiting lure: plugging it in can install malware. The safe step is to hand it, unplugged, to the security team, who can examine it safely and warn staff if more turn up. The lost-and-found box is the runner-up: it keeps the stick off the finder's computer, but the next person may plug it in, and security never hears of it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because returning lost items is kind. But plugging in an unknown stick can run malicious code, which is exactly what baiting relies on.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it keeps the stick out of use. But security never learns of the attempt, so they cannot check for more sticks or warn staff.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it keeps the stick off the finder's computer. But whoever opens the box may plug it in, and the security team never hears of the lure.

tips: Eliminate: A plugs an unknown device into a work computer, and B disposes of it so security never learns of the attempt.
Final two: D beats C because lost-and-found passes the risk to the next person; the security team can examine it safely and warn others.
Exam cue: unknown media found at work may be a lure; hand it to security and never plug it in.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining); NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1 (Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Leaving a tempting item, such as a memory stick labeled "salaries", for someone to pick up and use' (notes 2.3.3 Social Engineering Tactics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.question: Attackers take over a long-standing supplier's real email account and use it to ask a cheese maker's accounts clerk to send future payments to a new bank account. Which term names this attack MOST precisely?

options.A: A whaling attack
options.B: A business email compromise attack
options.C: A quishing attack
options.D: A spear phishing attack on the clerk

questions.key_concept: Business email compromise uses a real or faked business email account to redirect payments or change bank details.
questions.pre_read: Notice whose account sends the request and what it asks for.
questions.correct_explanation: Business email compromise (BEC) uses a real or faked business email account, here a supplier's hijacked one, to request payments or bank-detail changes. Spear phishing is the runner-up: the message does target one clerk, but BEC names the more precise pattern of a trusted business account redirecting money. Whaling targets senior leaders, and quishing uses quick response (QR) codes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the attack aims at money. But whaling targets senior executives, and this request goes to an accounts clerk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it is another phishing variant. But quishing uses a quick response (QR) code to reach a fake site; no code appears here.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the clerk is a chosen target. But a hijacked supplier account redirecting payments is business email compromise, the more precise name.

tips: Eliminate: A targets senior leaders, and C relies on QR codes; neither fits a clerk's payment email.
Final two: B beats D because the request comes from a real supplier account and redirects payments, which is what BEC names.
Exam cue: name the variant by its channel, its target or its method; a trusted business account redirecting money is BEC.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Uses a real or faked business email account to request payments or changes to bank details' (notes 2.3.4 Phishing and Its Variants). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 4, 1 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2.3 Security awareness. AI-boosted phishing and deepfakes
questions.question: Attackers who took over a toy maker's executive's phone number used an artificial intelligence (AI) cloned voice to pass a clerk's callback for a large payment. What should the security manager propose as BEST?

options.A: Repeat the callback on the same number before paying
options.B: Require a second staff member to approve large payments
options.C: Train clerks to listen for signs of a cloned voice
options.D: Ask executives to remove recorded talks from public sites

questions.key_concept: When one check, such as a callback, can be beaten, add a control needing two people, such as two sign-offs on large payments.
questions.pre_read: Notice which check the attacker already beat, and how.
questions.correct_explanation: Callbacks to known numbers remain a good check, but this one failed because the attacker controlled the number. Requiring a second staff member to approve large payments means one deceived person cannot send money alone, whoever the caller seems to be. Training clerks to listen for cloned voices is the runner-up: awareness helps, but good clones are hard to hear, and one fooled clerk still pays the attacker.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a repeat check feels thorough. But it uses the same number the attacker controls, so the same cloned voice answers again.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: clerks should know cloned voices exist. But good clones are hard to hear, and a fooled clerk still pays unless a second person must approve.
