questions.question: A planetarium's indicator for admin accounts lacking MFA turns amber; the security manager owns the risk, but band rules have the access analyst open a fix ticket at amber. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Send the security manager a ticket to decide on a fix
options.B: Move the amber line up until the indicator reads green
options.C: Raise the fix ticket for the admin accounts lacking MFA
options.D: Recheck the admin accounts daily until the band turns red

questions.key_concept: Each threshold band names an action and an owner; when the rule assigns the amber action to the practitioner, they take it without waiting.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the band rules assign at amber, and to whom.
questions.correct_explanation: Thresholds turn numbers into action: each band names what happens and who does it. At amber, the rules give the access analyst the job of raising the fix ticket, so they do it now. Sending it to the security manager is the runner-up: the manager owns the risk, but the rules already assign the amber step to the analyst, so routing it upward only adds delay.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the security manager owns the risk. But the band rules assign the amber action to the analyst; asking the owner to decide it delays a step already assigned.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because green looks better. But moving a threshold hides the risk without reducing it, and only the threshold's owner may change it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because amber is not yet red. But each band names its own action; waiting for red skips the amber step meant to stop the rise.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the line instead of reducing the risk, and D waits for red when the amber band already names an action.
Final two: C beats A because the band rules give the amber action to the analyst; owning the risk does not mean taking every step.
Exam cue: when a threshold rule assigns an action to your role, take it; escalate only what the rule sends upward.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Color bands show how close a metric is to its limit; each band names an action and an owner' (notes 2.4.4 Thresholds, Targets and Escalation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A paper mill's quarterly security report to leaders lists 12 metrics with no commentary, and leaders ask what they are expected to do. Which addition is BEST for the security manager to make?

options.A: A brief section on causes, naming the decisions leaders face
options.B: A color-coded status and target beside each metric
options.C: A link to the live dashboard, letting leaders drill down
options.D: An appendix holding the raw data behind every metric

questions.key_concept: Reports for leaders explain causes and state the decisions needed; status grids, live dashboards and raw data serve other needs.
questions.pre_read: Consider what the leaders asked for, and which format delivers it.
questions.correct_explanation: Leaders asked what they need to do, and a report's strength is context, causes and recommendations. A brief section explaining what drives the results and naming the decisions needed answers them directly. Color-coded status against targets is the runner-up: it shows at a glance which metrics are off track, but not why, or what the leaders should decide.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: status at a glance helps leaders spot problems. But it shows which metrics are off track, not why, or what decision leaders must make.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because drill-down shows everything. But live dashboards suit teams acting daily; leaders need conclusions and decisions, not more charts to explore.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it supports transparency. But raw data adds detail, not meaning; it leaves leaders to work out the causes and decisions themselves.

tips: Eliminate: C hands leaders an operations tool, and D adds raw detail; neither tells them what to decide.
Final two: A beats B because leaders asked what to do; color-coded status shows what is off track, not the decisions needed.
Exam cue: match the format to the audience; leaders need causes, trends and decisions, operators need live detail.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.2 (Measurement Reporting: reports give context, such as the risk indicated and what action or decision may be needed); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OV-03 (organizational cybersecurity risk management performance is evaluated and reviewed for adjustments needed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Scorecards suit periodic reviews against targets; reports explain trends, causes and the decisions needed' (notes 2.4.5 Dashboards, Scorecards and Reports). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and option B reworded. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: distractor C given a comma-ing tail so that shape does not point only to the key.

questions.subtopic: 2.4 Measuring effectiveness. Using measurement to improve
questions.question: A tram operator's average time to disable leavers' accounts doubled in March after a steady year, and the IT manager urges buying an identity governance tool at once. What should the security analyst propose FIRST?

options.A: Find the cause behind the March figure's rise
options.B: Buy the tool now and replace the manual leaver steps
options.C: Raise the leaver target so the March figure falls within it
options.D: Drop March from the trend as a one-month outlier

questions.key_concept: Before acting on a metric's sudden change, find out why it moved; the cause decides the right fix.
questions.pre_read: Think about what could make one month's figure jump.
questions.correct_explanation: A sudden change in a metric is a question, not an answer: the March jump could come from a data error, a one-off batch of leavers or a missed HR notice, and each needs a different fix. Finding the cause first means the money goes to the real problem. Buying the tool is the runner-up: it acts quickly, but if bad data or a one-off batch drove March, the spend fixes nothing.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it acts quickly on what looks like a decline. But the cause is unknown; if bad data or a one-off batch drove March, the tool fixes nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the figure would look on target. But changing the target to fit a bad month hides the problem and improves nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because one month can be noise. But dropping a bad month unexamined hides what may be a real problem; it needs explaining, not deleting.

tips: Eliminate: C moves the target to fit a bad result, and D deletes the bad month instead of explaining it.
Final two: A beats B because the cause decides the fix; buying before knowing why the number moved may spend money on the wrong problem.
Exam cue: when a metric jumps, ask why before acting; check the data and the cause, then choose the fix.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.4 (Data Quality: a validation process checks the integrity and accuracy of measures data before analysis); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OV-03 (organizational cybersecurity risk management performance is evaluated and reviewed for adjustments needed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Look at trends, not one month alone, and ask why a number moved before acting' (notes 2.4.6 Using Measurement to Improve). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026; re-set from patch times to leaver accounts after the cross-domain gate (cc_d2_042 uses patch times). Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): 'metrics analyst' became 'security analyst' (canonical role names). Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and option B reworded.

questions.question: A city's AI permit-review assistant has risk indicators for accuracy and input drift, but only its data scientists see them, in their own notebooks. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Add the indicators to the main risk dashboard, each with an owner
options.B: Have the data scientists tell the risk owner when they feel concerned
options.C: Replace the indicators with the assistant's monthly uptime figure
options.D: Keep them with the data scientists, who know the model best

questions.key_concept: AI risk indicators belong in the same dashboards and escalation paths as other risks, with owners and thresholds, not in a specialist's private view.
questions.pre_read: Think about who needs to see an AI risk before anyone can act on it.
questions.correct_explanation: AI risks should be managed like other critical risks, so their indicators belong on the main risk dashboard, each with an owner, thresholds and an escalation path, where leaders can see and act on them. Having the data scientists tell the risk owner when concerned is the runner-up: it reaches the owner, but it rests on one team's judgment, with no thresholds or routine view.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it gets news to the risk owner. But it relies on one team's judgment of when to speak, with no thresholds or regular view for leaders.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because uptime is easy to report. But uptime shows the assistant answers, not that its answers are right or its inputs still match training.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because they know the model. But AI risks belong with other risks, where leaders see them; keeping them private leaves no one accountable to act.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps accuracy for uptime, which says nothing about answer quality, and D keeps AI risk out of leaders' sight.
Final two: A beats B because indicators on the main dashboard, with owners and thresholds, trigger action by rule, not by one team's judgment.
Exam cue: treat AI risk indicators like any other KRI: visible, owned, thresholded and escalated.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MEASURE 2.4 (the functionality and behavior of the AI system are monitored when in production); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) Section 1.2.4 (Organizational Integration and Management of Risk: AI risks are treated along with other critical risks)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Each AI KRI has an owner, thresholds and an escalation path, like any other KRI' (notes 2.4.7 AI Risk Indicators). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 5, 4 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A sports nutrition brand's security analyst is explaining its new governance, risk and compliance (GRC) program to leaders. Which output is MOST typical of the program's risk management part?

options.A: A compliance report, with evidence for each obligation
options.B: A risk register, with a treatment plan for each risk
options.C: A risk appetite statement, signed off by the board
options.D: A policy set, with a named owner for each policy

questions.key_concept: Risk management's main output in GRC is a risk register with treatment plans, worked within the appetite that governance sets.
questions.pre_read: Recall the main question each of the three GRC parts answers, and what each one produces.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk management finds, rates and treats risks to the business's goals, so its main output is a risk register with a treatment plan for each risk. The appetite statement is the runner-up: it is about risk, but the board sets it as a governance decision, and risk management works within the limit it sets rather than producing it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because compliance shares the GRC records. But evidence that obligations are met is the compliance part's output, not risk management's.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it concerns risk. But the board sets appetite as a governance decision; risk management then rates and treats risks within that limit.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because policies guide risk work. But approving policies and naming their owners is governance, the part that sets direction and accountability.

tips: Eliminate: A is the compliance part's output, and D is governance work, which sets policies and their owners.
Final two: B beats C because risk management rates and treats risks inside limits that leaders set; the appetite statement itself is a governance decision.
Exam cue: match each GRC part to its output: governance sets direction and limits, risk management keeps the register, compliance keeps the evidence.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk management finds, rates and treats risks to goals within limits leaders set, and keeps the register and treatment plans' (notes 2.1.1 GRC Purpose and Importance). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A hat maker's only felt supplier is shut for six weeks after a fire, though the hat maker's own systems and workshop are unharmed. What should its continuity coordinator do FIRST?

options.A: Ask IT to bring the order system up at the recovery site
options.B: Ask the incident response team to open a security incident
options.C: Follow the business's own plan for losing a key supplier
options.D: Wait for the supplier's own recovery to restore deliveries

questions.key_concept: Business continuity covers everything critical functions depend on, including key suppliers; disaster recovery restores technology and data.
questions.pre_read: Think about which kinds of disruption each plan is built to handle.
questions.correct_explanation: Business continuity keeps critical functions running through any disruption, including the loss of a key supplier, so the coordinator turns to the hat maker's own plan, with its alternate sources or stock. Waiting for the supplier's recovery is the runner-up: the supplier may well recover, but six weeks without felt halts production, and the hat maker cannot direct another firm's plan.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a fire caused the disruption. But bringing systems up at a recovery site is disaster recovery, and the hat maker's systems are working.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the event is a disruption. But incident response handles security incidents, and a fire at a supplier's factory is not one.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the supplier's recovery matters. But six weeks without felt stops production, and the hat maker cannot run another firm's plan; its own continuity plan covers this loss.

tips: Eliminate: A restores technology that still works, and B opens a security incident for a supplier's fire, which is not one.
Final two: C beats D because the hat maker's own continuity plan covers losing a key supplier; waiting on another firm's recovery leaves production stopped.
Exam cue: continuity plans cover people, places, suppliers and communication, not just systems; when the technology is fine, think business continuity.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 2.2 (Types of Plans: Business Continuity Plan and Disaster Recovery Plan); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-2 (Contingency Plan)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The BC plan covers the whole business, including people, workplaces and suppliers' (notes 2.2.2 Business Continuity vs Disaster Recovery). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): stem no longer names the continuity coordinator ('Which plan should it use') (removed the 'continuity' echo); A and B now carry the hat maker's possessive so length no longer marks the final two. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): re-angled from 'which plan type' to the coordinator's first action, because cc_d2_007 already tests the DR/BC/IR classification with the same option set (rule 8). Key C says 'the business's' rather than 'the hat maker's', so the stem's organization name is not echoed only in the key (rule 10).

questions.question: Interviewers at a polling firm get automated calls in a recorded voice, claiming to be the firm's bank, asking them to key in their corporate card numbers. Which term names this attack MOST precisely?

options.A: A vishing attack
options.B: A smishing attack
options.C: A whaling attack
options.D: A quishing attack

questions.key_concept: Vishing is phishing by voice call, including recorded or AI-generated voices, while smishing uses text messages.
questions.pre_read: Recall how phishing variants are named by the channel they use or the people they target.
questions.correct_explanation: Vishing is phishing by voice call, including recorded or artificially generated voices, so automated calls asking staff to key in card numbers fit it exactly. Smishing is the runner-up: it also reaches staff through their phones, but it arrives as a text message, not as a call.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it also targets people through their phones. But smishing uses text messages; these lures arrive as recorded voice calls.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the calls chase company money. But whaling targets senior executives, and these calls go to the firm's interviewers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is another phishing variant. But quishing uses quick response (QR) codes that lead to fake websites, not phone calls.

tips: Eliminate: C needs senior executives as the target, and D needs a quick response (QR) code; neither appears here.
Final two: A beats B because the lure arrives as a voice call; smishing is the same trick sent as a text message.
Exam cue: name phishing variants by channel or target: texts are smishing, calls vishing, QR codes quishing, executives whaling.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Vishing is phishing by voice call, including recorded or artificially generated voices' (notes 2.3.4 Phishing and Its Variants). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A campsite operator's two parks both report 'critical patches applied within 14 days', but one counts from each patch's release and the other from when IT logged it. What should the security analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Average the two parks' figures into one monthly result
options.B: Footnote the difference and keep reporting both methods
options.C: Agree one written counting rule with both parks
options.D: Report whichever park's method gives the better figure

questions.key_concept: Measures must be collected the same way everywhere and every period, so a metric needs one written definition before figures are compared.
questions.pre_read: Think about what makes two sites' figures for the same metric comparable.
questions.correct_explanation: A metric is only comparable when every site measures it the same way, so the first step is one written counting rule that both parks follow. Then the trend and the 14-day target mean the same thing everywhere. Footnoting the difference is the runner-up: it is honest, but the figures still measure different things, so no one can compare the parks or track a single trend.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because one figure is simpler. But averaging two figures measured in different ways produces a number that describes neither park.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it discloses the gap. But the two methods still measure different things, so the parks' figures and trends stay incomparable.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it flatters the program. But choosing the method by its result is gaming the metric, and it hides real patch delays.

tips: Eliminate: A averages figures that measure different things, and D picks the method by its result, which games the metric.
Final two: C beats B because one shared counting rule makes the figures comparable; a footnote only explains why they are not.
Exam cue: a metric needs one written definition and collection method everywhere it is used, or its trends and targets mean nothing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.2 (Characteristics of Measures: consistency, time-based reference and replicability)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Collect data the same way every period, so trends mean something' (notes 2.4.1 Measures and Metrics: The Basics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): 'metrics analyst' became 'security analyst' (canonical role, auditor rule 11).

questions.question: A laundry chain's video policy, owned by its operations director, keeps video 30 days unless legally held and assigns its deletion to the system administrator. How should the administrator BEST handle expired, unheld video?

options.A: Archive the expired video offline, recording its location
options.B: Ask the operations director to approve each deletion first
options.C: Delete the expired video on schedule, logging each deletion
options.D: Move the expired video to cheaper cloud storage for a year

questions.key_concept: A retention obligation sets when data must go as well as how long it stays; with no legal hold, expired data is deleted on schedule.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a retention period requires once it ends.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy sets a 30-day limit, no legal hold applies and the task is assigned to the administrator, so deleting the expired video on schedule, with a record, meets the obligation. Retention rules limit how long data is kept, not only how short. Asking the director to approve each deletion is the runner-up: the director owns the policy, but has already decided, and the policy gives the task to the administrator.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because keeping a copy feels safer. But video kept past its limit breaks the policy and holds personal images that should be gone.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the director owns the policy. But the policy already sets the limit and assigns deletion, so asking again only delays it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it keeps storage costs low. But moving the video still keeps it past its limit, breaking the policy as much as keeping it.

tips: Eliminate: A and D both keep video past its 30-day limit, which breaks the retention policy wherever the copy is stored.
Final two: C beats B because the owner already set the rule and assigned deletion to the administrator; asking for each approval only delays it.
Exam cue: retention limits work both ways; when the period ends, no hold applies and the task is yours, delete on schedule and keep a record.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-122 Section 4.2.1 (Minimizing the Use, Collection, and Retention of PII: destruction follows retention schedules and litigation holds); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Identify each obligation, its source and what it requires, and meet it as work happens, including retention limits' (notes 2.1.4 Compliance Obligations and Evidence). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): 'IT technician' became 'system administrator' (canonical role names). Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and option A reworded. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: distractor A given a comma-ing tail so that shape does not point only to the key.

questions.question: A swim school's onboarding gives new instructors a general security course, but nothing on the children's booking records they open from day one. Which change is BEST for the awareness lead?

options.A: Hang posters about locking screens in the pool office
options.B: Add a quiz to the end of the general course
options.C: Email new instructors a note listing rules for children's records
options.D: Add a module on handling children's records to the course

questions.key_concept: Training matches the role: staff whose job involves a sensitive kind of data get role-based training on it, beyond the general course and awareness.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the onboarding already covers and what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: Training builds the skills a job needs, on top of what every employee gets. Instructors open children's booking records from day one, so a module on handling those records teaches the real risks of their role while they are new. The emailed note is the runner-up: it shares the rules early, but a list of rules is an awareness message and does not build the skill the way training does.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because posters keep security visible. But one reminder about one habit is awareness for everyone; it says nothing about handling children's records.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a quiz checks what staff learned. But the general course has no content on children's records, so a quiz can only test what it already teaches.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it reaches new instructors on day one. But a list of rules is an awareness message; role-based training gives instructors practice in handling the records their job involves.

tips: Eliminate: A is a single-habit awareness reminder for everyone, and B tests the general course without adding what it lacks.
Final two: D beats C because a module trains instructors in handling the records their role uses; an emailed list of rules is awareness, not training.
Exam cue: when a role handles data the general course does not cover, add role-based training for that role; awareness messages support training but never replace it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-3 (Role-based Training); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 10.2 (Awareness and Training: raising awareness, building job skills and building in-depth knowledge)
