questions.question: A pasta maker's IT manager wants to buy a hot site for every system now and run the business impact analysis (BIA) later to confirm the choice. Which proposal from the continuity coordinator is BEST?

options.A: Sign the vendor's quote now and fine-tune it after the BIA
options.B: Rank the servers by importance and move the top ones first
options.C: Finish the BIA, then match sites to its recovery targets
options.D: Buy a hot site for the top-earning order system alone

questions.key_concept: The business impact analysis comes before recovery choices, so each function's recovery targets decide which sites and backups it needs.
questions.pre_read: Think about the order of the steps in continuity planning.
questions.correct_explanation: The BIA comes before recovery choices: it shows which functions need recovery in hours and which can wait days, so recovery targets, not a vendor quote, decide what each site must do. Buying a hot site only for the order system is the runner-up: it trims the cost, but it still guesses which function matters most before the BIA has measured the impact.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the quote is ready. But buying first lets the purchase set the targets, and a hot site for every system likely overspends.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it looks systematic. But the BIA starts from business functions, not servers; ranking servers misses people, suppliers and manual steps.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it narrows the spend. But revenue alone is a guess at criticality; the BIA first measures how harm grows for every function.

tips: Eliminate: A lets a purchase set recovery needs before they are known, and B starts from servers instead of business functions.
Final two: C beats D because the BIA measures every function's impact before any site is chosen; picking the top earner is still a guess.
Exam cue: BIA first, then recovery targets, then sites and backups; an option that buys a solution before the BIA is out of order.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2 (Conduct the Business Impact Analysis (BIA): BIA results feed strategy development for the BCP and DRP); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2.1 (Determine Business Processes and Recovery Criticality: MTD, RTO and RPO)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The BIA starts from business functions and comes before choosing recovery sites or backup schedules' (notes 2.2.3 Business Impact Analysis (BIA)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A ski rental chain's IT team wants a measure of how often its booking servers break down, not how long repairs take. Which measure fits this goal BEST?

options.A: Mean time between failures (MTBF)
options.B: Mean time to recover after a failure (MTTR)
options.C: Mean time to detect a fault (MTTD)
options.D: Recovery time objective (RTO)

questions.key_concept: Mean time between failures shows how often systems fail; mean time to recover shows how long recovery takes.
questions.pre_read: Recall the difference between measures of how often something fails and how long it takes to fix.
questions.correct_explanation: Mean time between failures tracks the average time between breakdowns, so it shows how often the servers fail. Mean time to recover is the runner-up: it is a common measure for the same servers, but it tracks how long recovery takes after a failure, which the team said it does not want here.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it measures the same servers' outages. But MTTR tracks how long recovery takes after a failure, not how often failures happen.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because detection is part of handling outages. But MTTD tracks how long a problem exists before it is found, not how often servers fail.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it concerns outages. But the RTO is a target the business sets for restoring a function, not a measure of failures.

tips: Eliminate: C measures how long problems go unnoticed, and D is a recovery target, not a measure of how often failures occur.
Final two: A beats B because MTBF tracks the time between breakdowns; MTTR tracks how long each recovery takes.
Exam cue: between failures means how often; to recover or repair means how long to fix; to detect means how long a problem hides.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: mean time between failures tracks the average time between system breakdowns)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Mean time to recover is how long recovery takes on average; failure frequency is mean time between failures (MTBF)' (notes 2.4.2 Types of Security Measures). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A honey producer's register entry for an unpatchable printer has an owner, a control and a tolerance, but nothing shows when the risk nears that tolerance. Which addition should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: A second control linked to the printer entry in the register
options.B: A wider tolerance that the printer risk fits within
options.C: A yearly review of the entry by its risk owner
options.D: A risk indicator with alert levels set from the tolerance

questions.key_concept: A risk register entry needs an indicator with alert levels set from its tolerance, so the owner learns when the risk nears its limit.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a register entry needs to show a risk moving toward its limit.
questions.correct_explanation: A register entry links each risk to an owner, its controls, a tolerance and an indicator. Without the indicator, nothing shows the risk drifting toward its limit, so an indicator whose alert levels come from the tolerance lets the owner act in time. A yearly review is the runner-up: the owner does look again, but between reviews the risk can pass its tolerance unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more controls lower risk. But a second control does not show where the risk stands against its tolerance.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the risk would then sit within limits. But leaders set tolerance; widening it to fit the risk hides the risk without reducing it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: an owner's review keeps the entry current. But a yearly look gives no warning in between, so the risk can pass its tolerance unseen.

tips: Eliminate: A adds protection without showing where the risk stands, and B moves the limit instead of watching the risk.
Final two: D beats C because an indicator warns as the risk nears its tolerance; a yearly review can miss months of change.
Exam cue: a complete register entry has an owner, controls, a tolerance and an indicator that warns before the tolerance is crossed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 2.4 (Metrics: key risk indicators and key performance indicators)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The risk register links each risk to a tolerance, an owner, its controls and an indicator' (notes 2.1.7 Tolerances and the Risk Register in GRC). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): stem says 'signals' instead of 'warns' to soften the echo with the key's 'alert levels'. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): stem reworded so 'that tolerance' has a clear referent ('nothing signals as the risk nears it' was ungrammatical).

questions.subtopic: 2.3 Security awareness. AI-boosted phishing and deepfakes
questions.question: In a video interview, a skateboard maker's HR coordinator sees a remote candidate's face blur and lag behind their voice; procedure sends suspected hiring fraud to the security team. What should the coordinator do FIRST?

options.A: Accuse the candidate of using a deepfake and end the call
options.B: Ask to see the candidate's ID card on camera, then carry on
options.C: Score the answers and leave identity to the security team's later checks
options.D: Finish politely and pass the concern to the security team

questions.key_concept: AI can fake faces and voices on live video, so suspected deepfake fraud follows the set procedure rather than on-the-spot checks.
questions.pre_read: Think about what AI can now fake on a live video call.
questions.correct_explanation: AI tools can now put a fake face on a live video call, and the procedure routes suspected hiring fraud to the security team, who can check identity properly. So the coordinator finishes politely, without tipping off the candidate, and passes the concern on. Asking to see an ID card is the runner-up: it looks like a check, but a card held up on a video that may itself be faked proves little.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it confronts the fraud. But the lag may be innocent, and accusing the candidate alerts a real impostor; the procedure sends it to security.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it tries to confirm identity. But a card shown on a possibly faked video proves little, and the procedure assigns checks to security.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the security team does check identity later in hiring. But the procedure sends suspected fraud to them now, and waiting lets a possible impostor move further through hiring.

tips: Eliminate: A accuses someone on uncertain signs, and C defers a possible deepfake that the procedure says to pass on now.
Final two: D beats B because the procedure gives identity checks to the security team; an ID card shown on a possibly faked video proves little.
Exam cue: when AI could be faking what you see and hear, follow the procedure for the suspicion instead of improvising your own test.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) Section 2.8 (Information Integrity: deepfakes and content that impersonates others); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PS-3 (Personnel Screening)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Deepfake video puts a familiar or invented face on a live call; defenses rely on process' (notes 2.3.5 AI-Boosted Phishing and Deepfakes). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): option C now names the security team too, so the stem's owner is no longer echoed only in the key (rule 3).

questions.question: A ceramics wholesaler's IT team built its order system's recovery in a cloud provider's region, and the IT manager tells the security analyst it still needs regular failover tests. How should the analyst BEST respond?

options.A: Disagree, as the provider's uptime promise covers recovery
options.B: Agree, but leave the testing to the provider under contract
options.C: Disagree, as cloud copies are ready to run whenever needed
options.D: Agree, as only a test shows the cloud recovery works

questions.key_concept: Only a test shows a cloud recovery setup works, and the customer still owns its data, settings and recovery.
questions.pre_read: Think about what moving recovery to a cloud provider changes, and what it does not.
questions.correct_explanation: Moving recovery to a cloud region changes where the order system comes back, not whether it will: only a failover test shows that the copies, settings and steps actually restore it. Under shared responsibility, the provider runs the platform, but the wholesaler owns its data, settings and recovery. Leaving testing to the provider is the runner-up: the wholesaler's own team built this setup, so the wholesaler must prove its own system comes back.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because providers publish uptime targets. But uptime covers the provider's platform, not whether the wholesaler's own system and data restore.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it accepts that testing matters. But the wholesaler's own team built the setup and owns its data, settings and recovery, so it must test its own failover.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because cloud resources start quickly. But copies, settings and steps can be wrong or missing until a test shows they work.

tips: Eliminate: A mistakes the provider's platform uptime for the customer's recovery, and C assumes untested copies will simply work.
Final two: D beats B because the customer still owns its data and settings, so it must test its own failover instead of leaving it to the provider.
Exam cue: moving recovery to the cloud changes where it runs, not who must prove it works; an untested recovery is a hope, not a plan.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.5 (Plan Testing, Training, and Exercises); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-4 (Contingency Plan Testing)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Cloud recovery means paying mainly for stored copies until a failover, and it still needs testing' (notes 2.2.6 Recovery Sites). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): stem states the wholesaler's own team built the setup (rules out a provider-run service as a second answer); key says a test shows recovery works rather than makes it work. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): the claim now comes from the IT manager instead of 'a colleague', so the speaker's role no longer predicts whether a claim is right (cross-domain role tell); correct explanation now leads with the tested principle instead of the notes' cost line. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: role 'junior analyst' became 'security analyst'.

questions.question: A tea house chain's key risk indicator (KRI) dashboard turned red last month and no one acted; its legend explains only what each color means. Which fix should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Assign each band a named responder plus a set action
options.B: Lower the red line and send warnings sooner
options.C: Email each red reading to the whole company
options.D: Ask the risk owner to check the dashboard each week

questions.key_concept: Each threshold band should name an owner and a set action, so crossing it triggers a response by rule.
questions.pre_read: Think about what turns a colored band on a dashboard into an actual response.
questions.correct_explanation: Thresholds turn numbers into action only when each band says who acts and what they do, such as amber opening a fix ticket and red reaching the risk owner the same day. Then a red reading triggers a response by rule. A weekly check by the risk owner is the runner-up: someone looks, but nothing is set to happen at each band, and a red reading can sit for days.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because earlier warnings sound safer. But a lower line only produces more readings that no one is assigned to answer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because everyone will see it. But a message to all staff gives no one the duty to act, so the reading still goes unanswered.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it brings an owner's attention. But a weekly look sets no action for each band, so a red reading can wait for days.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the line without making anyone act, and C tells everyone but gives the response to no one.
Final two: A beats D because each band then triggers a named person's set action; a weekly look leaves red readings waiting.
Exam cue: a threshold works only when each band names who acts and what they do; without that, the colors are decoration.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.2 (Measurement Reporting: reports give context, such as the risk indicated and what action or decision may be needed); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Color bands show how close a metric is to its limit; each band names an action and an owner' (notes 2.4.4 Thresholds, Targets and Escalation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): 'metrics analyst' became 'security analyst' (canonical role, auditor rule 11). Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and option B reworded.

questions.question: A violin maker's security manager is drafting the new governance, risk and compliance (GRC) program's charter for senior management to approve. Which content does the charter MOST need?

options.A: The security controls in use, with their test steps
options.B: The program's purpose, scope, authority and sponsor
options.C: The settings departments must apply to their systems
options.D: The obligations the program covers and who owns them

questions.key_concept: A GRC program charter states the program's purpose, scope, authority and sponsor, and senior management approves it.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a program charter is for, and which details belong in other documents.
questions.correct_explanation: A charter is a short approved document stating why the program exists, what it covers, what authority it has and which senior sponsor backs it. Once senior management approves it, the program can ask every department for time and evidence. The obligations list is the runner-up: the program needs one, with an owner for each duty, but it is a working document kept current as duties change, not what gives the program authority.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because controls are what the program manages. But control test steps belong in procedures and test plans, not in the document that authorizes the program.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because departments must apply settings. But system settings belong in standards and baselines under the program's policies, not in its charter.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the program needs an obligations list with owners. But that list is a working document kept current as duties change; the charter states purpose, scope, authority and sponsor.

tips: Eliminate: A puts control test steps in the charter and C puts system settings in it; both belong in lower-level documents.
Final two: B beats D because the charter authorizes the program through its purpose, scope, authority and sponsor; the obligations list is working detail kept beside it.
Exam cue: a charter answers why, what, under whose authority and backed by whom; controls, settings and duty lists live in other documents.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PM-1 (Information Security Program Plan); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Charter: a short approved document stating a program's purpose, authority, scope and sponsor' (notes 2.1.2 Planning a GRC Program, key term). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 2: re-angled from 'who approves' because cc_d1_036 already teaches that lesson with the same option layout. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): removed 'before any work starts', which contradicted notes 2.1.2's order (obligations listed before the charter is approved) and cc_d2_091; 'GRC lead' became 'security manager' (canonical role); A, C and D lost their 'every/each' quantifiers so the key is not the only option without one.

questions.question: A visitor tells a student housing provider's desk clerk they are a fire inspector needing a list of residents' rooms; procedure says only the data owner releases resident data. What is the clerk's BEST response?

options.A: Print the list now and tell the data owner afterward
options.B: Check the visitor's inspector badge and print the list
options.C: Call the fire department on its published number, then print the list
options.D: Decline politely and pass the request to the data owner

questions.key_concept: Pretexting uses a believable story and claimed authority; the defense is following procedure, such as sending data releases to the data owner.
questions.pre_read: Think about the tactic a visitor claiming official authority is using.
questions.correct_explanation: Claimed authority and a believable story are classic pretexting pressure, and the procedure leaves releases of resident data to the data owner. So the clerk declines politely and passes the request on, whoever the visitor turns out to be. Calling the fire department is the runner-up: checking through a published number is sound, but even a real inspector's request still goes to the data owner for release.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the owner still hears of it. But telling the owner after the release skips the approval the procedure requires, and inspections are a common pretext.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a badge looks like proof. But badges are easy to fake, and the clerk is not the person who may release resident data.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it checks the claim through a trusted number. But even a genuine inspector's request goes to the data owner, who alone releases resident data.

tips: Eliminate: A releases the data before the owner approves, and B treats a badge as proof, though only the data owner may release the data.
Final two: D beats C because only the data owner may release resident data; confirming the visitor's story does not move that decision to the clerk.
Exam cue: claimed authority is a pressure signal; whatever the story, a data release follows the release procedure and its owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Information Owner/Steward)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Attackers build a believable story and apply pressure such as authority; the defense is to follow procedure' (notes 2.3.3 Social Engineering Tactics). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and options B, C reworded. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded with 'and', which A and B also have, instead of a comma-ing tail.

questions.question: A dog-walking app relies on an outside provider's AI model to match walkers with clients, and its risk owner wants a key risk indicator (KRI) for continuity risk from that dependency. Which measure BEST fits?

options.A: Accuracy of the provider's AI model on a weekly labeled sample
options.B: Outage hours of the provider's AI service each month
options.C: Uptime of the app's own web servers each month
options.D: Share of clients who rate their walker five stars

questions.key_concept: AI risk indicators must match the named risk; outages at an AI provider signal continuity risk, while accuracy signals drift.
questions.pre_read: Think about which AI risk is named here and which measure warns of it.
questions.correct_explanation: Continuity risk from an outside AI provider shows in how often and how long that provider's service fails, so a rising trend in its outages warns that matching may stop. Match accuracy is the runner-up: it is a sound AI risk indicator, but it warns of model drift, a quality risk, not of losing the service the app depends on.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it is a real AI risk indicator. But accuracy warns of model drift; the risk named here is losing the provider's service.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because uptime sounds like continuity. But the app's own servers can run perfectly while the outside AI service is down.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it shows how well matches work for clients. But satisfaction is a business performance figure and gives no warning of provider outages.

tips: Eliminate: C watches the app's own servers, not the outside provider, and D tracks client satisfaction, not dependency risk.
Final two: B beats A because the named risk is losing the provider's service; accuracy warns of drift, a different AI risk.
Exam cue: match each AI indicator to its named risk: accuracy and input shift for drift, override rates for quality, provider outages for continuity.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 3.1 (AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored, and risk controls are applied and documented); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 2.4 (Metrics: key risk indicators and key performance indicators)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Use of unapproved AI tools shows policy risk; AI service outages, including at providers, show continuity risk' (notes 2.4.7 AI Risk Indicators). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded.

questions.question: A hearing aid maker's high-availability pair of order servers sits side by side in one server room, and leaders want orders to survive a fire there. Which change should the system administrator propose as BEST?

options.A: Add a third server to the pair in the same room
options.B: Add fire suppression to the room that holds both servers
options.C: Give each server mirrored disks using RAID 1
options.D: Move the standby server to a room in another building

questions.key_concept: Redundancy works only if the spare does not share the failure; for a site-wide event such as fire, put the spare elsewhere.
questions.pre_read: Think about which failures two servers in the same room still share.
questions.correct_explanation: Redundancy only protects against failures the spare does not share. Two servers side by side fall to the same fire, so moving the standby to another building lets orders fail over when the room is lost. Fire suppression is the runner-up: it limits damage, but a fire, smoke or a suppression discharge can still take the room, and both servers, out of service.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more servers mean more spares. But a third server in the same room is lost to the same fire.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it reduces fire damage. But a fire or a suppression discharge can still shut the room, taking both servers down together.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because RAID is a form of redundancy. But it protects against a failed disk, not a fire that destroys both servers.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a spare that shares the same room, and C guards against disk failure, not the loss of the room.
Final two: D beats B because separating the servers removes the shared point of failure; suppression only limits the damage to it.
Exam cue: match the spare's distance to the event: another rack for a rack failure, another building for a fire, another region for a regional disaster.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-7(1) (Alternate Processing Site | Separation from Primary Site); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR-03 (mechanisms are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Put spares in another building or region when a whole site could be lost' (notes 2.2.1 Redundancy and High Availability). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A review approved a kitchen remodeling firm's AI transcription tool for both meetings and sales calls; sales staff have now started using it on calls. What should the analyst keeping the AI inventory do FIRST?

options.A: Ban sales from every AI tool until a new policy exists
options.B: Record the call use in the inventory after a review approves it
options.C: Log the call use in the inventory under the existing approval
options.D: Ask the vendor to review how the tool stores call recordings

questions.key_concept: An AI approval covers the uses and data it names; uses inside it are recorded, and only uses outside it go back for review.
questions.pre_read: Think about what an AI tool's approval actually covers.
questions.correct_explanation: The approval names customer calls as well as meetings, so this use is already inside what was vetted. The analyst records it in the inventory under the existing approval, keeping the record complete. Recording it only after a review is the runner-up: review is right for a use that no approval covers, but this one was vetted, so a repeat review only delays an accurate inventory.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI tools can leak data. But this use is approved, and a blanket ban pushes staff toward hidden tools.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: uses outside an approval go back for review. But this approval names customer calls, so no review is due; the inventory records uses as they start.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because call storage matters. But the organization's review already covered calls, and a vendor cannot approve or reopen a use.

tips: Eliminate: A bans every AI tool over a use that is approved, and D asks the vendor to settle a question the organization's review has already decided.
Final two: C beats B because the approval names customer calls, so the use is covered and recorded now; a fresh review is for uses that no approval covers.
Exam cue: read what an AI approval names; uses inside it are recorded, and only uses with new data or purposes go back for review.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 1.6 (mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'An AI inventory records each use and its owner; a use that no approval covers is reviewed before it starts' (notes 2.1.8 Governing AI Use). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 2 (5 Nov 2026): stem now says the approval names sales staff's customer calls (removes the ambiguity a blind tester found); option B now logs the use only after a fresh review, instead of being the key plus an extra step (rule 5). Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): B also says 'in the inventory', so the stem's 'inventory' is no longer echoed only in the key (rule 10), and opens with 'Record' so B and C no longer start with the same words; stem states the approved uses outright; 'IT support analyst' became 'help desk analyst' (canonical role); B's explanation no longer implies an uncovered use is kept out of the inventory (cc_d5_038). Stem clarified (5 Nov 2026, blind re-test) so the call use reads as already approved.

questions.question: A wedding venue's events manager asks a sales assistant for their password, so the manager can check the assistant's bookings during two weeks of leave. Which response from the assistant is BEST?

options.A: Keep it private and point the manager to IT for access
options.B: Share it, then change the password after returning from leave
options.C: Leave it in a sealed envelope in the manager's desk drawer
options.D: Share it with the manager, who already oversees the bookings

questions.key_concept: Passwords are never shared, even with a manager; someone who needs access gets it in their own name from IT.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a password proves.
questions.correct_explanation: A password proves who is acting, so it is never shared, even with a manager. IT can give the manager access to the bookings in their own name, which keeps every action traceable. Sharing it and changing it later is the runner-up: it limits how long the password is exposed, but for two weeks the manager's actions would look like the assistant's.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: changing it later limits exposure. But for two weeks the manager acts as the assistant, and their actions cannot be told apart.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a sealed envelope feels controlled. But it still hands over the password, and anyone who opens the drawer can use it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the manager has a real need. But authority over the work does not entitle anyone to another person's password; IT can grant access.

tips: Eliminate: C still hands over the password in another form, and D treats the manager's authority as a reason to share it.
Final two: A beats B because IT can grant the manager access in their own name; sharing, even briefly, makes the manager's actions look like the assistant's.
Exam cue: never share a password, even with a manager or IT; when someone needs access, the answer is access in their own name.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PL-4 (Rules of Behavior)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Never share a password, even with IT or a manager' (notes 2.3.6 Password and Passphrase Habits). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: option D reworded.

questions.question: A timber merchant's monthly security scorecard for department managers shows only this month's figures. Which change BEST helps the managers judge progress?

options.A: Show each figure beside its target, plus the last few months
options.B: Replace the monthly scorecard with a live hourly dashboard
options.C: Add server-level figures to leave nothing out
options.D: Color each figure green or red and drop the numbers

questions.key_concept: Scorecards for managers show each figure against its target and recent trend, so progress, not just status, is visible.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a manager needs beside a single month's figure to judge progress.
questions.correct_explanation: Managers tracking goals need status against targets over time, so each figure should sit beside its target and the last few months. Then a manager can see whether a number is improving or slipping, not just where it stands. The live dashboard is the runner-up: it suits teams who act daily, but managers review progress periodically and still need targets and trends.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: dashboards show current data well. But managers review progress monthly, and an hourly view still lacks targets and trends.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more data seems more complete. But server-level detail buries the few figures managers need to judge progress.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because colors read quickly. But without numbers, targets or trends, managers cannot see how far off a figure is or which way it moves.

tips: Eliminate: C buries managers in operations detail, and D removes the numbers they need to judge how far off each figure is.
Final two: A beats B because managers judge progress against targets over time; a live dashboard suits daily operators, not monthly reviews.
Exam cue: show trends and targets, not single snapshots, and fit the format to the audience: dashboards for operators, scorecards for managers.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.2 (Characteristics of Measures: consistency, time-based reference and replicability); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 1.4 (Document Terminology: measures are quantifiable values and metrics track progress with respect to a set target)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Scorecards suit periodic reviews against targets; show trends, not single snapshots' (notes 2.4.5 Dashboards, Scorecards and Reports). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and option C reworded.

questions.question: While mapping a hot sauce maker's controls to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, its security analyst finds backups run but no restore has been tested. How should the analyst BEST record the backup outcome?

options.A: As fully met, since a backup control is linked
options.B: As partly met, with the untested restores listed as a gap
options.C: As not applicable, since backups already run nightly
options.D: As met, with a note asking IT to begin restore tests soon

questions.key_concept: A framework mapping records what is actually achieved; a control that meets only part of an outcome leaves a tracked gap.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the framework's backup outcome asks for.
questions.correct_explanation: The CSF outcome for backups covers creating, protecting, maintaining and testing them, so backups that have never been restored meet only part of it. Recording it as partly met, with the missing tests logged as a gap, keeps the mapping honest and gets the gap an owner. Marking it met with a note is the runner-up: it flags the tests, but it reports the outcome as achieved before it is.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a control is linked. But a link shows intent, not achievement; the outcome includes testing, which has never happened.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because backups clearly matter here. But not applicable means the outcome does not fit the firm; this one fits and is only partly done.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it flags the missing tests. But marking the outcome met overstates progress, and a note is easier to lose than a tracked gap.

tips: Eliminate: A counts a linked control as proof the outcome is met, and C misuses not applicable for an outcome that clearly fits.
Final two: B beats D because the outcome includes testing, so it is only partly met; recording it as met overstates progress.
Exam cue: in a framework mapping, record what is actually achieved; a partial control is a tracked gap, not a met outcome with a note.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested); NIST CSF 2.0 Section 3.1 (CSF Profiles: Organizational Profiles are used to understand, tailor, assess, prioritize and communicate outcomes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Load the framework, link each control to the items it meets, and treat only real gaps as needing new work' (notes 2.1.5 Choosing and Mapping Frameworks in GRC). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and option C reworded; role 'compliance analyst' became 'security analyst'. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded with 'with' instead of a comma-ing tail.

questions.question: Ransomware has encrypted a music streaming startup's main subscriber database, the plan's trigger for disaster recovery, which the IT director declares. What should the incident response lead do FIRST?

options.A: Keep containing and tell the IT director the trigger is met
options.B: Finish containment and eradication, then tell the IT director
options.C: Restore the database from last night's backup straight away
options.D: Declare the disaster themselves; the trigger has been met

questions.key_concept: Activation triggers move a response into disaster recovery; the incident lead reports a met trigger to whoever declares, while containment continues.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a plan's activation trigger is for.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan names encryption of the main database as the disaster recovery trigger and gives the declaration to the IT director, so the lead tells the director while containment carries on in parallel. Recovery can then be planned against its time targets. Finishing containment first is the runner-up: containment matters, but holding back a trigger that is already met spends recovery time the business may not have.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: containment must go on. But the trigger is already met, and holding the news until eradication ends delays recovery the business may need.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a backup exists. But restoring before containment risks reinfection, and recovery starts only once the IT director declares it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the trigger really is met. But the plan gives the declaration to the IT director; the lead's job is to report the trigger, not declare.

tips: Eliminate: C restores into systems the ransomware may still reach, and D takes a declaration the plan gives to the IT director.
Final two: A beats B because the trigger is already met, so the director must hear of it; containment and recovery planning run side by side.
Exam cue: when an incident meets a plan's activation trigger, tell whoever declares and keep containing; response and recovery overlap, they do not queue.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 4.2.1 (Activation Criteria and Procedure: if an activation criterion is met, the designated authority should activate the plan); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 2.2 (Types of Plans: Business Continuity Plan and Disaster Recovery Plan)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'An incident that meets a plan's trigger goes to whoever declares; containment carries on while recovery starts' (notes 2.2.2 Business Continuity vs Disaster Recovery). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): relabeled from the AI-assisted resilience sub-topic (2.2.9) and the 'flagged by AI monitoring' phrase removed, because the AI fact played no part in the decision; the item tests plan activation, now taught in 2.2.2. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded without a semicolon; distractor D now carries one.

questions.subtopic: 2.4 Measuring effectiveness. Using measurement to improve
questions.question: Procedure has a laser tag chain's security analyst check big swings before the security manager's report goes out, and the simulated phishing click rate fell from 15% to 0%. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Report the drop to leaders as a training success
options.B: Ask the security manager whether to publish the drop
options.C: Verify the click data and that the emails reached staff
options.D: Retire the click-rate metric now, as its target is met

questions.key_concept: A sudden metric improvement needs its data checked as much as a sudden decline, before anyone reports it as success.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a sudden swing in a metric can mean.
questions.correct_explanation: A fall from 15% to 0% in one cycle is as suspicious as a sudden rise, and the procedure gives the check to the analyst. Verifying the click data, and that the simulation emails reached staff at all, comes before anyone reports success. Asking the security manager is the runner-up: they own the report, but the procedure has already assigned this check to the analyst.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a lower click rate sounds like progress. But a sudden fall to zero needs checking first; blocked or miscounted emails can produce it.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the security manager owns the report. But the procedure assigns checking big swings to the analyst, so the analyst checks first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the figure looks perfect. But a target that seems met may rest on bad data, and retiring the metric would hide the problem.

tips: Eliminate: A reports an unchecked figure as success, and D retires the metric on a number nobody has verified.
Final two: C beats B because the procedure gives big-swing checks to the analyst; the owner decides on publication once the data is verified.
Exam cue: a sudden improvement deserves the same scrutiny as a sudden drop; check the data behind it before anyone celebrates.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.4 (Data Quality: a validation process checks the integrity and accuracy of measures data before analysis)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Treat a sudden improvement with the same curiosity as a sudden drop; check the data behind a metric before trusting it' (notes 2.4.6 Using Measurement to Improve). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Fix-up round 3 (5 Nov 2026): 'metrics analyst' became 'security analyst' (canonical role, auditor rule 11).

questions.question: A toll road operator's continuity plan counts its AI plate reader as up while servers respond, though accuracy fell from 98% to 81% after new plate designs. Which proposal is BEST for its continuity coordinator?

options.A: Add a second server so that the reader stays available
options.B: Count the reader as down below an agreed accuracy level
options.C: Hand the accuracy drop to the incident response lead
options.D: Add the accuracy figure to the monthly status report

questions.key_concept: An AI service that drifts below acceptable accuracy is effectively down, so continuity plans define availability by output quality too.
questions.pre_read: Think about whether an AI service that answers wrongly is really available.
questions.correct_explanation: A model can fail slowly while every server looks healthy, and a reader at 81% accuracy is effectively down for the tolling that relies on it. Counting it as down below an agreed accuracy level makes the plan's fallback start when quality fails, not only when servers stop. Reporting the figure monthly is the runner-up: it makes the drift visible, but nothing in the plan acts on it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because redundancy protects availability. But a second server runs the same drifting model, so the wrong reads continue on both.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because something has gone wrong. But drift caused by new plate designs is not a security incident; it is a continuity and model issue.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it makes the drift visible. But a monthly figure triggers nothing, so the plan still treats a failing reader as up.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a server that runs the same drifting model, and C treats model drift as a security incident.
Final two: B beats D because an accuracy floor makes the plan act when quality fails; a monthly report only records it.
Exam cue: for AI services, available means giving usable answers; build accuracy into the plan's idea of down, not just server uptime.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MEASURE 2.4 (the functionality and behavior of the AI system are monitored when in production); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 2.4 (mechanisms are in place and responsibilities assigned to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI systems that perform inconsistently with intended use)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A drifting model that gives wrong answers is effectively down for the process that relies on it' (notes 2.2.8 Backing Up AI Systems and Model Drift). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A science center's staff report suspicious emails with a button but never hear what happened next, and reports have fallen for three months. Which change should the awareness lead propose as BEST?

options.A: Make reporting mandatory, with penalties for misses
options.B: Thank each reporter, sharing the threats their reports caught
options.C: Swap the button for a longer form that asks for more detail
options.D: Run more phishing simulations, giving staff practice at reporting

questions.key_concept: Reporting grows when it is quick, safe and acknowledged; thanking reporters and sharing results keeps staff reporting.
questions.pre_read: Think about what keeps people willing to report after the first few times.
questions.correct_explanation: People keep reporting when it feels worthwhile, so thanking each reporter and sharing what their reports caught closes the loop. Silence makes staff assume their reports vanish. More simulations is the runner-up: practice builds the habit of spotting lures, but it does not fix the missing feedback that is draining staff's will to report.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because rules can force behavior. But penalties make people hide mistakes, and fear damages the reporting culture.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more detail helps analysts. But extra steps make reporting harder, so even fewer people will bother.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: practice builds the reporting habit. But the drop follows silence after reports, and more drills leave that silence unchanged.

tips: Eliminate: A punishes people, which drives reports down, and C adds friction to a route that should be quick.
Final two: B beats D because reports are falling for lack of feedback; more practice does not tell anyone their reports mattered.
Exam cue: a healthy reporting culture is quick, safe and rewarded; thank reporters and show them the result.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 Section 2.5.1 (All Users: incentivize behavioral change in positive, non-punitive ways); NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Developing a Cybersecurity and Privacy Culture: the culture should emphasize, reinforce and drive desired behaviors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Give people one simple way to report, then thank them and share the outcome' (notes 2.3.7 Reporting Culture and Phishing Simulations). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 6, 5 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and option D reworded. Word-tell sweep round 2, 18 Nov 2026: distractor D given a comma-ing tail so that shape does not point only to the key.

questions.question: A rug importer's IT and compliance teams each keep their own risk list, and leaders get two conflicting ratings for the same order system. Which change should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Have the board pick one team's rating for each system
options.B: Load both teams' risk lists into one GRC platform
options.C: Keep one shared risk register that both teams work from
options.D: Ask compliance to rate every risk, as it is audited

questions.key_concept: GRC gives leaders one shared view of risk: teams work from one register, so the same risk is not rated two ways.
questions.pre_read: Recall why GRC joins governance, risk and compliance instead of running them separately.
questions.correct_explanation: GRC joins governance, risk and compliance so they share one set of records and leaders get one view of risk. A single register that both teams work from removes the conflicting ratings at their source. Loading both lists into a platform is the runner-up: a tool can hold the data, but two separate lists inside it still give leaders two answers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the board oversees risk. But asking leaders to referee duplicate records keeps the silos; the fix is one shared record, not a choice between two.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a GRC platform can hold shared records. But two separate lists loaded into it still rate one system two ways; tools support GRC, they do not join it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because compliance work leaves evidence. But giving one team every rating keeps a one-sided view instead of joining both teams' knowledge in one record.

tips: Eliminate: A has leaders referee duplicate records instead of fixing them, and D hands every rating to one team because its work is audited.
Final two: C beats B because GRC means one shared record of risk; two lists loaded into one platform still disagree.
Exam cue: when separate teams give leaders conflicting pictures, the GRC answer joins them into one shared record, not a tool or a tiebreak.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Chapter One (The Need for Integrated Organization-Wide Risk Management: missions, processes and systems require an integrated, organization-wide view for managing risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'All three share one set of records, so one control can meet several needs' (notes 2.1.1 GRC Purpose and Importance). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A water-testing lab copies its results database at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00, against a 4-hour recovery point objective (RPO). After a 17:00 failure, which finding should the system administrator report as MOST accurate?

options.A: Five hours of results are lost, which is past the RPO
options.B: One hour of results is lost, well inside the RPO
options.C: As many as six hours of results are lost, beyond the RPO
options.D: No results are lost after the database comes back

questions.key_concept: Data lost in a failure runs back from the moment of failure to the last good copy; compare that span with the RPO.
questions.pre_read: Recall which direction the RPO is measured in, and from which point.
questions.correct_explanation: The RPO looks back from the failure to the last good copy. The last copy before 17:00 was taken at 12:00, so five hours of results are lost, beyond the 4-hour RPO; a six-hour copy cycle cannot meet it. Six hours is the runner-up: that is the worst case the schedule allows, not what this 17:00 failure loses.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the 18:00 copy is only an hour away. But data loss is counted back to the last copy taken; a copy due after the failure never happened.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: six hours is the most this schedule could ever lose. But this failure came five hours after the 12:00 copy, so five hours are lost.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a restore brings the database back. But it brings back only what the 12:00 copy holds; results recorded after it are gone.

tips: Eliminate: B counts forward to a copy that was never taken, and D assumes a restore returns data made after the last copy.
Final two: A beats C because loss is measured from this failure back to the 12:00 copy; six hours is only the schedule's worst case.
Exam cue: for data loss, count back from the failure to the last good copy; RPO is about data, looking back.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2.1 (Determine Business Processes and Recovery Criticality: MTD, RTO and RPO)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, the business can lose; it looks back from the disruption' (notes 2.2.4 Recovery Objectives: MTD, RTO and RPO). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): re-set from a dance school's bookings to a water-testing lab's results, reported by the system administrator, so it no longer retells cc_d2_054's frame; losing words 'once' and 'is' removed from distractors.

questions.question: An adult missing from a camp's parent-signed pickup list comes for a child, naming the coach and saying a parent sent them; procedure releases children only to listed adults. What should the counselor do FIRST?

options.A: Release the child to the adult who knows the coach by name
options.B: Ask the child whether a parent sent this adult, then decide
options.C: Ask the camp director to add the adult to the list now
options.D: Keep the child with office staff while calling a parent

questions.key_concept: Pretexting uses a believable story; where a person's safety is involved, staff follow the release procedure exactly, whatever the story.
questions.pre_read: Recall how pretexting works and what a written procedure is for.
questions.correct_explanation: The pickup list is the camp's safeguard for children, and knowing a coach's name proves research, not authority. The counselor keeps the child safe with staff and calls a listed parent, who can confirm the story or come. Asking the director to add the adult is the runner-up: it feels like sensible escalation, but parents sign the list, so a name added on the adult's own story carries no parent's permission.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the adult knows real details. But a coach's name is easy to learn; knowing it proves research, not that a parent sent them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because children often know family plans. But a child's word is not a parent's permission, and a child can know an adult who must not collect them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it brings in someone senior. But parents sign the list; a name added now, on the adult's own story, carries no parent's permission.

tips: Eliminate: A treats knowing the coach's name as proof, and B treats a child's word as a parent's permission.
Final two: D beats C because parents sign the pickup list; a name added on the adult's own story carries no parent's permission.
Exam cue: when a person's safety is at stake and a story applies pressure, follow the written procedure exactly; details and claims prove nothing.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining)

questions.question: A furniture rental firm is starting its first security measurement program and has little reliable data yet. Which type of measure should the security analyst propose starting with as BEST?

options.A: Impact measures, such as revenue lost in each hour of outage
options.B: Efficiency measures, such as average time to detect incidents
options.C: Effectiveness measures, such as share of test phishing emails reported
options.D: Implementation measures, such as share of laptops with encryption on

questions.key_concept: New measurement programs start with implementation measures, then broaden to effectiveness, efficiency and impact as their data matures.
questions.pre_read: Recall the four types of security measures and what data each one needs.
questions.correct_explanation: Measurement guidance has programs gather implementation measures first: they record whether controls are in place, and the data is easy to collect. Once those are in hand, the program broadens to effectiveness, efficiency and impact. Effectiveness is the runner-up: it shows whether controls work, which matters, but it needs reliable data the firm does not have yet.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because executives care most about business impact. But impact measures need mature data linking security events to outcomes, which a new program lacks.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because speed matters. But average detection times need consistent processes and records over time before the figures mean anything.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it shows whether a control works. But effectiveness measures come after implementation data, and the firm does not yet have reliable data.

tips: Eliminate: A needs data linking security to business outcomes, and B needs consistent timing records; a brand-new program has neither.
Final two: D beats C because programs first record which controls exist, then broaden to whether they work.
Exam cue: a new measurement program starts with implementation measures, then adds effectiveness, efficiency and impact as data matures.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.3.1 (Implementation Measures: once implementation measures are completed, the program broadens to effectiveness, efficiency and impact measures); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.3 (Types of Measures: implementation, effectiveness, efficiency and impact)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Programs usually start with implementation measures and add the others as data matures' (notes 2.4.2 Types of Security Measures). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bowling chain maps its controls to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0; a grant now requires SP 800-53. Where should the security analyst look FIRST for the SP 800-53 controls behind each CSF outcome?

options.A: The CSF tiers, which rate how rigorous practices are
options.B: The chain's risk register, listing its current risks
options.C: The informative references that map CSF 2.0 to SP 800-53
options.D: The SP 800-53 catalog, read one control at a time

questions.key_concept: NIST's informative references map CSF 2.0 outcomes to documents such as SP 800-53, so a second mapping starts from them.
questions.pre_read: Recall what NIST publishes alongside CSF 2.0 to link its outcomes to other standards.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST publishes informative references alongside CSF 2.0 that link each outcome to controls in other documents, including SP 800-53. Starting there shows which SP 800-53 controls support each outcome the chain already maps, so the analyst checks those links and adds controls only for real gaps. Reading the SP 800-53 catalog is the runner-up: it is the right document, but working through it one control at a time repeats a mapping NIST has already published.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tiers are part of CSF 2.0. But they describe how rigorous the organization's risk practices are overall; they do not link outcomes to SP 800-53 controls.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the register drives control choices. But it lists risks, not how CSF outcomes line up with SP 800-53 controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the grant names SP 800-53. But reading it one control at a time redoes a mapping NIST already publishes, and it is slow.

tips: Eliminate: A rates practice maturity rather than linking frameworks, and B lists risks; neither shows which SP 800-53 controls support a CSF outcome.
Final two: C beats D because the informative references already link CSF outcomes to SP 800-53; start from them rather than rebuilding the mapping by hand.
Exam cue: when a second framework is required, start from the published mapping (informative references or a crosswalk), then reuse controls and close only the real gaps.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 4 (Introduction to Online Resources That Supplement the CSF: Informative References map Core outcomes to standards such as SP 800-53)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'NIST publishes informative references that map CSF 2.0 outcomes to other documents, such as SP 800-53, so a new mapping can start from them' (notes 2.1.5 Choosing and Mapping Frameworks in GRC). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. questions.question: An aquarium's staff receive what looks like last week's genuine newsletter, resent from the usual sender, but its link leads to a different site. Which term should the security analyst use as MOST precise?

options.A: A whaling attack
options.B: A clone phishing attack
options.C: A pharming attack
options.D: A spear phishing attack

questions.key_concept: Clone phishing resends a copy of a genuine earlier message with its link or attachment swapped for a malicious one.
questions.pre_read: Recall how phishing variants are named: by channel, by target or by method.
questions.correct_explanation: Clone phishing copies a real message the targets already received, such as last week's newsletter, and swaps its link or attachment for a malicious one, so familiarity does the persuading. Spear phishing is the runner-up: it is targeted too, but it is written fresh from research about the victims, not copied from a genuine earlier message.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because whaling is a targeted variant. But whaling aims at senior executives, and this resent newsletter went to staff in general.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because users land on a fake site. But pharming redirects traffic through poisoned DNS or device settings, not through a changed link in an email.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it reaches known recipients. But spear phishing is crafted fresh from research; copying a real earlier message is what defines clone phishing.

tips: Eliminate: A targets senior executives, and C redirects traffic through DNS or settings rather than a changed link in an email.
Final two: B beats D because the message is a copy of a real earlier email with its link swapped; that copying is the defining feature.
Exam cue: name a phishing variant by its defining feature: channel (smishing, vishing), target (whaling) or method (clone, credential harvesting).
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining)
