questions.question: An ice rink's AI model forecasts skate rentals; since late-night sessions began, its forecasts have steadily worsened, though nobody changed the model or its training data. Which cause should the system administrator suspect MOST?

options.A: A fault in the servers that host and run the model
options.B: Poisoning of its training data by an outside attacker
options.C: Drift as live rental demand moved away from the training data
options.D: Prompt injection hidden in the text of customers' online bookings

questions.key_concept: Model drift is a gradual drop in accuracy as live data moves away from what the model learned, with no tampering involved.
questions.pre_read: Recall the ways an AI model can start giving worse answers, and what each one needs.
questions.correct_explanation: Model drift is a gradual loss of accuracy as real-world data moves away from what the model learned. New late-night sessions changed rental patterns, and nothing else changed. Poisoning is the runner-up: it also degrades a model, but it needs someone to tamper with the training data, and the stem rules that out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because outages stop services. But the model still produces forecasts; they are wrong, not missing, which points to its data rather than its servers.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: poisoning does make a model less accurate. But it requires tampered training data, and no one changed the data here.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because injected text can mislead AI. But prompt injection targets models that follow text instructions, not a demand forecast, and it would not cause a steady slide.

tips: Eliminate: A would stop the forecasts rather than make them wrong, and D targets models that follow text instructions, not a demand forecast.
Final two: C beats B because the slide began with a change in the real world while the training data stayed untouched.
Exam cue: a steady accuracy slide after the world changes, with nothing tampered, points to drift; watch accuracy and keep a fallback ready.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) Appendix B (How AI Risks Differ from Traditional Software Risks: data, model or concept drift can trigger corrective maintenance); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MEASURE 2.4 (the functionality and behavior of the AI system are monitored when in production)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Model drift is a gradual drop in accuracy as real-world data moves away from what the model learned' (notes 2.2.8 Backing Up AI Systems and Model Drift). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): 'IT technician' became 'system administrator' (canonical role names). Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key reworded.

questions.question: A bookbinder's risk owner proposes late payroll runs as the early-warning key risk indicator (KRI) for late or missed payroll when one staff member is away. Which reply from the security analyst is BEST?

options.A: Agree; late runs show the risk most directly
options.B: Disagree; count payroll tasks that have no trained backup
options.C: Agree; and add on-time payroll runs as a second KRI
options.D: Disagree; count the hours of payroll training given each year

questions.key_concept: A KRI can count a people exposure, such as tasks only one person can do; counting the risk event itself only confirms past harm.
questions.pre_read: Recall the difference between leading and lagging indicators, and between KPIs and KRIs.
questions.correct_explanation: An early-warning KRI must move before harm happens. Late runs are counted only after payroll has already slipped, so they warn too late. Tasks with no trained backup are the exposure that turns an absence into a late payroll, and the count falls as cover is trained. Agreeing with late runs is the runner-up: they fit the named risk, but they are a lagging measure.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: late runs are tied to the named risk. But they record harm after it happens; an early-warning KRI must move before payroll is late.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more indicators feel safer. But on-time runs judge process performance, a KPI, and the lagging measure stays as the KRI.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training builds cover. But hours delivered count activity, not whether any payroll task still depends on one person.

tips: Eliminate: C adds a performance measure and keeps the lagging one, and D counts training activity rather than exposure.
Final two: B beats A because late runs count harm after it happens; tasks with no trained backup warn before it.

Exam cue: if the proposed KRI counts the risk event itself (late payroll for a late-payroll risk), it is lagging; count the condition that makes the event possible, including work that depends on one person.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 2.4 (Metrics: key risk indicators and key performance indicators)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Good KRIs are leading, measurable and tied to a named risk, with thresholds set from its tolerance' (notes 2.4.3 Key Performance and Key Risk Indicators). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): key concept and exam cue re-centred on people exposure (single-person dependency) so the item no longer repeats cc_d2_016's lesson.

questions.question: An exhibition center's RACI chart for badge-access reviews lists facilities and IT staff as Responsible but no one as Accountable; the security manager assigns owners. What should the analyst drafting the chart do FIRST?

options.A: Mark the security manager and facilities manager both Accountable
options.B: Mark the facilities manager Accountable, as their team does most work
options.C: Ask the security manager to name one Accountable person
options.D: Treat the Responsible staff as answering for the result

questions.key_concept: Each task has exactly one Accountable person; when none is named, the gap goes to whoever assigns owners.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each RACI letter means and how many of each a task can have.
questions.correct_explanation: Every task needs exactly one Accountable person, and assigning owners is the security manager's call here, so the analyst raises the gap for them to decide. Marking the facilities manager is the runner-up: it fills the box with one name, but the analyst would be choosing an owner without authority, and doing most of the work makes a team Responsible, not Accountable.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it names both managers involved. But two Accountable people each assume the other is acting; each task gets exactly one.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it gives the task one Accountable name. But the security manager assigns owners, and doing the work makes a team Responsible, not Accountable.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the work is already assigned. But Responsible people do the work; without one person answering for the result, missed reviews have no owner.

tips: Eliminate: A makes two people Accountable, and D confuses doing the work with answering for the result.
Final two: C beats B because the security manager assigns owners; the analyst raises the gap instead of choosing an owner.
Exam cue: when a task has no clear owner, raise it with whoever assigns owners; never fill the gap by quietly deciding yourself.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Each task has exactly one Accountable person; several can be Responsible' (notes 2.1.3 GRC Accountability: RACI and Reporting Lines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A podcast studio's staff are moving their work passwords into the company's password manager. Which protection for each person's vault should the help desk analyst stress as MOST important?

options.A: Reuse the strong work email password as the master password
options.B: Change the master password each quarter
options.C: Use a long master passphrase backed by MFA
options.D: Use a long master passphrase and a short auto-lock timer

questions.key_concept: A password manager is only as safe as its vault: protect it with a long master passphrase and multifactor authentication.
questions.pre_read: Recall current advice on password length, reuse and forced changes.
questions.correct_explanation: The vault holds every password, so its own lock matters most: a long master passphrase plus multifactor authentication (MFA) means a stolen or guessed master password alone cannot open it. A long passphrase with a short auto-lock timer is the runner-up: auto-lock guards an unattended device, but if the passphrase is phished or captured by malware, nothing else stands between the attacker and every stored password.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the email password is already strong. But reuse means one leak opens both the mailbox and every password in the vault.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because changing passwords sounds careful. But forced periodic changes lead to predictable variants; change the master password when exposure is suspected.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: auto-lock protects a vault left open on an unattended device. But a phished or captured passphrase still opens the vault from anywhere; only a second factor stops that.

tips: Eliminate: A ties the vault to a password used elsewhere, and B forces quarterly changes that push people toward predictable variants.
Final two: C beats D because MFA stops a phished or captured passphrase from opening the vault; auto-lock only covers an unattended device.
Exam cue: guard the one secret that protects all the others most strongly: a long passphrase plus MFA, changed on any sign of exposure.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-63B-4 Section 3.1.1.2 (Password Verifiers: no periodic changes, but a forced change on evidence of compromise); NIST SP 800-63B-4 (Authentication and Authenticator Management: multi-factor authentication)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A password manager stores unique passwords; protect it with a strong passphrase and multifactor authentication (MFA)' (notes 2.3.6 Password and Passphrase Habits). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): D no longer a subset of the key (auto-lock runner-up); B loses 'every'. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: key and option B reworded.

questions.question: A board-game publisher's key risk indicator (KRI) for servers without a tested backup reaches amber; band rules send amber to the risk owner and red to senior management. What should the security analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Pass the amber reading and its trend to the risk owner
options.B: Escalate the reading straight to senior management as a rising risk
options.C: Raise the amber line so the reading shows green again
options.D: Hold the reading from the risk owner until it turns red

questions.key_concept: Each threshold band names an owner and an action; a reading goes to the owner its band names, no higher and no lower.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a threshold band's color tells you to do, and whom to tell.
questions.correct_explanation: Each threshold band names an action and an owner, so an amber reading goes to the risk owner, who can act before the risk reaches red. Escalating to senior management is the runner-up: it looks diligent, but the band rules reserve senior management for red, and skipping the owner takes the decision from the person accountable for the risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the risk is rising. But the rules send amber to the risk owner; senior management is the red-band path, and the owner decides first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because green looks better. But moving a line hides the risk without reducing it, and only the threshold's owner may change it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because amber is not yet a breach. But amber exists to reach the risk owner early; holding it until red wastes the warning the band rules give.

tips: Eliminate: C moves the line instead of reducing the risk, and D sits on a warning the band rules say to act on.
Final two: A beats B because the band rules route amber to the risk owner; senior management is the red-band path.
Exam cue: follow the band rule exactly: each color names who hears about it and what happens, no higher and no later.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.2 (Measurement Reporting: reports give context, such as the risk indicated and what action or decision may be needed); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PM-6 (Measures of Performance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Color bands show how close a metric is to its limit; each band names an action and an owner' (notes 2.4.4 Thresholds, Targets and Escalation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: At a freight forwarder, the customs team's head tells the security analyst that security steps in customs processing are IT's job, not the customs team's. Which reply from the analyst is MOST accurate?

options.A: Agree; IT runs the security tools and owns the steps
options.B: Agree; the security team answers for each security step
options.C: Disagree; each team owns the security steps in its processes
options.D: Disagree; the risk owner carries out the steps in each process

questions.key_concept: Security is part of everyone's job: each team carries out the security steps in its own processes, and its head answers for them.
questions.pre_read: Recall who carries out security steps in day-to-day work.
questions.correct_explanation: Security is part of everyone's job. IT runs shared tools such as email filtering, but the security steps inside a team's own process, such as verifying a caller before changing a shipment's delivery address, belong to that team, and its head answers for them. IT owning the steps is the runner-up: IT does own its tools, but it cannot carry out checks inside every other team's daily work.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: IT does run the security tools. But checks inside the customs process are done by customs staff; IT cannot perform them for every team.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the security team leads the program. But it sets policy and advises; it cannot carry out steps inside every team's daily work.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because risk owners decide how a risk is treated. But deciding is not doing; the steps inside a process are carried out by the team that runs it.

tips: Eliminate: B hands every step to the security team, and D confuses deciding on a risk with doing the work.
Final two: C beats A because IT owns its tools, not the checks inside another team's process; the customs team does those.
Exam cue: security is part of everyone's job; whoever runs a process carries out the security steps inside it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving); NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Developing a Cybersecurity and Privacy Culture: the culture should emphasize, reinforce and drive desired behaviors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Security is part of everyone's job, not only the security team's' (notes 2.3.1 Security Culture and Leadership). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): setting moved from an insurance broker's claims team to a freight forwarder's customs team (setting overuse); D now names 'process' so the stem's processing is not echoed only in the key; B loses 'every' (now 'each'). A loses 'so'.

questions.question: A lantern maker's restore test met its recovery time objective (RTO), but the restored data was 30 hours old against a 24-hour recovery point objective (RPO). How should the continuity coordinator BEST record it?

options.A: Record a pass, since the restore met the RTO
options.B: Record no result before a full interruption test runs
options.C: Ask the system owner whether missing the RPO counts as a pass
options.D: Record a failure, since the data missed the RPO

questions.key_concept: A restore test passes only when data comes back complete, within the RTO and no older than the RPO allows.
questions.pre_read: Recall the two recovery targets a restore test is checked against.
questions.correct_explanation: A restore test checks that data comes back intact, in time and recent enough. Thirty-hour-old data breaks the 24-hour RPO, so the lantern maker would lose more orders than it accepts, however fast the restore. Grading tests is the coordinator's task, so they record the failure. Asking the system owner is the runner-up: owners decide how to close a gap, but here grading is the coordinator's job and the RPO already defines a pass.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the restore was fast. But speed is only half the test; data older than the RPO allows means more lost orders than the business accepts.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a bigger test seems more conclusive. But a full interruption is the riskiest test, and this restore test already gave a clear result.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the owner decides how to fix gaps. But grading tests is the coordinator's task, and the RPO already defines a pass.

tips: Eliminate: A checks only the time goal, and B swaps a clear result for the riskiest test there is.
Final two: D beats C because grading is the coordinator's task and the RPO already defines a pass; the owner then decides the fix.
Exam cue: a restore passes only if the data is complete, back within the RTO and recent enough for the RPO; when grading is your task, do it yourself.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-9(1) (System Backup | Testing for Reliability and Integrity); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.5 (Plan Testing, Training, and Exercises)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Choose the backup type and frequency to meet the recovery point objective (RPO)' (notes 2.2.5 Backups: Types, the 3-2-1 Rule and Restore Testing). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): sawmill became a lantern maker (setting overuse); 'the technician who grades tests' became the continuity coordinator (canonical role names); B loses 'until'.

questions.question: A cable TV provider's security analyst is copying green control statuses from the governance, risk and compliance (GRC) platform into a quarterly report. What should the analyst check FIRST?

options.A: Last quarter's statuses for the same controls
options.B: The date each control's data was last collected
options.C: Each control's named owner in the platform
options.D: The platform vendor's security certification

questions.key_concept: A GRC tool's status is only as current as its data; check when each feed last updated before trusting a green.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a dashboard color actually rests on.
questions.correct_explanation: A dashboard status is only as current as the data behind it. If a feed stopped months ago, a green shows an old result, so the analyst checks when each control's data was last collected before reporting it. A named owner is the runner-up: ownership matters in GRC, but it says nothing about whether today's green is still true.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because trends matter. But matching last quarter shows only that the colors agree; a stopped feed would repeat the same green.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: every control needs an owner. But an owner on record does not show that the status reflects current data.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a trusted platform seems reliable. But a certified tool still shows stale results when a data feed stops.

tips: Eliminate: A compares colors that a stopped feed would repeat, and D judges the tool rather than the data it is showing.
Final two: B beats C because a status is only as current as its data; ownership does not make a green true.
Exam cue: before trusting a dashboard green, check when its data was last collected; stale data gives stale colors.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.1 (Measures Documentation: recording when a measure was taken helps identify expired or invalid data); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.4 (Data Quality: a validation process checks the integrity and accuracy of measures data before analysis)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'A status is only as current as its data; check when each feed last updated before trusting a green' (notes 2.1.6 GRC Tools and Automation). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: An interpreting agency's awareness lead is deciding what happens when staff click the link in an approved phishing simulation. Which response to a click is BEST?

options.A: Lock the account and make the person retake the yearly course
options.B: Show a brief page pointing out the clues they missed
options.C: Enroll the person in the full yearly course again
options.D: Send the person's manager the names of everyone who clicked

questions.key_concept: In a phishing simulation, a click is a teaching moment: show the missed clues at once, without blame.
questions.pre_read: Recall what phishing simulations are for, and how they should treat a click.
questions.correct_explanation: A click in a simulation is a teaching moment. A brief page right after the click shows the clues the person missed while the lure is fresh, without blame, so they stay willing to report. Re-enrolling them in the full yearly course is the runner-up: it is training, but it comes late, repeats general content and feels like a penalty.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it forces training. But locking accounts punishes the click, and fear makes staff hide real mistakes instead of reporting them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it gives more training. But a long general course arrives late and feels like a penalty; a short, immediate explanation teaches more.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because managers can follow up. But naming clickers turns practice into blame, and reporting drops when people fear exposure.

tips: Eliminate: A and D punish or expose the clicker; simulations are practice, and fear of exposure lowers reporting.
Final two: B beats C because a short explanation at the moment of the click teaches while the lure is fresh, without feeling like a penalty.
Exam cue: simulations are practice; treat a click as a teaching moment, never as grounds for punishment or exposure.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 Section 2.7.2 (Experiential Learning: phishing exercises reviewed in advance, run at random and never punitive); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(1) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Practical Exercises)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Simulations are approved in advance, avoid lures that cause real distress and treat a click as a teaching moment, not grounds for punishment' (notes 2.3.7 Reporting Culture and Phishing Simulations). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): zoo became an interpreting agency (setting overuse); A loses 'until' and gains 'and', and the key says 'brief' (bank-wide word tells).

questions.question: A hop farm's AI tool sorting buyer feedback scored 97% accurate before launch; its model owner wants that figure reported monthly as the accuracy KRI. Which reply from the security analyst is BEST?

options.A: Disagree; check a sample of the latest live results monthly
options.B: Agree; the launch test is the most thorough figure
options.C: Agree; and rerun the same launch test set each month
options.D: Disagree; report the vendor's published accuracy monthly

questions.key_concept: AI accuracy indicators use recent, live results measured again each period; a one-time pre-launch score cannot warn of drift.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a risk indicator must do from one month to the next.
questions.correct_explanation: A key risk indicator must show how the risk is moving now. The 97% was measured once, before launch, so repeating it each month would stay flat while real accuracy slips. Checking a recent sample of live results each month reveals drift early. Rerunning the launch test set is the runner-up: it measures monthly, but the fixed test set never changes, so it cannot show the model falling behind new kinds of feedback.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the launch test was careful. But a one-time figure never changes, so as a monthly indicator it cannot warn that live accuracy is slipping.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it measures every month. But an unchanged model scores the same on a fixed test set, so the figure stays flat while live accuracy slips.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors test at scale. But the vendor's figure comes from its own data, not this farm's feedback, and it does not move with live results.

tips: Eliminate: B repeats a one-time launch score, and D swaps in a vendor figure from someone else's data; neither moves with live results.
Final two: A beats C because only live results show drift; a fixed test set scores the same while the world changes.
Exam cue: an AI accuracy indicator is measured on recent live results, period after period; a launch or vendor score is history, not a warning.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MEASURE 2.4 (the functionality and behavior of the AI system are monitored when in production)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Accuracy on recent, labeled live data, and shifts in live inputs away from the training data, tracked over time, signal model drift' (notes 2.4.7 AI Risk Indicators). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): museum's visitor feedback became a hop farm's buyer feedback (setting overuse). Key no longer the lone longest option (D lengthened).

questions.question: A rope-access firm's draft governance, risk and compliance (GRC) plan sets its scope, lists its obligations, picks a framework and has a funded, approved charter. Which gap should the security analyst flag as MOST important?

options.A: No GRC platform to hold the program's risks and controls
options.B: No vulnerability scan of every in-scope system
options.C: No external audit to show where it stands today
options.D: No named owner for each policy, risk and control

questions.key_concept: A GRC plan needs a named owner for each policy, risk and control; scope, framework and funding alone leave no one accountable.
questions.pre_read: Recall the planning steps for a GRC program, and what makes its work actually happen.
questions.correct_explanation: A GRC plan works only when every policy, risk and control has a named owner who answers for it; scope, obligations, a framework and a funded charter without owners leave nobody accountable for the work. The external audit is the runner-up: it can show where the firm stands, but its findings would go to a program with no one to act on them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tools organize GRC work. But a platform comes after the plan; without owners it would hold records nobody answers for.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because scans find real weaknesses. But scan results need owners and priorities before anyone acts on them; the plan's gap is accountability.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a baseline helps measure progress. But audit findings need owners to act on them, and the plan names none yet.

tips: Eliminate: A buys a tool before the plan is complete, and B produces results with no owners or priorities to act on them.
Final two: D beats C because an audit's findings need owners to fix them; accountability comes before measurement.
Exam cue: when a plan has scope, rules and funding but no owners, the missing piece is accountability: one named owner per item.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PM-1 (Information Security Program Plan)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Give each policy, risk and control an owner, and have senior management approve a charter and budget' (notes 2.1.2 Planning a GRC Program). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A housing charity's board chair says board members, as volunteers, need no security training, though emails built around their board roles keep targeting them. Which reply from the awareness lead is BEST?

options.A: Disagree; brief board members on the lures their power attracts
options.B: Agree; volunteers fall outside the staff training policy
options.C: Disagree; enroll board members in the yearly staff phishing course
options.D: Agree; the email filter already stops attacks on board members

questions.key_concept: Training follows role and risk, not employment status: anyone targeted for their position, volunteers included, needs training on the attacks aimed at them.
questions.pre_read: Recall who needs security training and how role-based training differs from the general course.
questions.correct_explanation: Volunteers or not, board members hold the authority attackers want, and the emails aimed at their roles show the risk is real. Training follows role and risk, so a short briefing on the attacks aimed at board roles fits them. Adding them to the staff course is the runner-up: it covers the basics, but not requests built around board roles, such as approving payments or sharing board papers.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because board members are not employees. But attackers target roles, not contracts; anyone with authority attackers want needs training that fits the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it brings the board into training. But the yearly staff course is built for everyone and misses the attacks aimed at board roles.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because filters stop much phishing. But these emails are already reaching board members, and a filter teaches no one to spot what gets through.

tips: Eliminate: B treats volunteer status as an exemption from risk, and D leans on a filter the stem shows is being passed.
Final two: A beats C because targeted roles need training on the attacks aimed at them; the staff course is the same for everyone.
Exam cue: training follows role and risk, not job title or pay: anyone attackers target for their position gets training on those attacks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-3 (Role-based Training); NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 Section 1.6.2 (Senior Leadership: leading by example and participating in their own training)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Match the learning to the role and the risk' (notes 2.3.2 Awareness, Training and Education). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): key no longer repeats the stem's 'targeting them'; runner-up C made as specific as the key.

questions.question: A milliner's AI monitor predicts a storage array failure, and the array's logs agree; the IT manager's runbook has the administrator switch to the tested standby on confirmed warnings. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Wait for a real failure, as AI predictions can be wrong
options.B: Keep running and restore from backup after any failure
options.C: Ask the IT manager to approve a move to the standby array
options.D: Move service to the standby array in a planned switch

questions.key_concept: Early detection is a resilience control: a confirmed warning lets the team switch to a spare before an outage happens.
questions.pre_read: Think about what an early, confirmed warning lets a team do before a failure.
questions.correct_explanation: Early detection is a resilience control: catching trouble before it disrupts the business leaves less to recover. The warning is confirmed, and the IT manager's runbook already gives the switch to the administrator, so a planned move avoids an outage. Asking the IT manager is the runner-up: it looks careful, but the runbook already holds the manager's approval, and waiting spends the warning.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI can be wrong. But the array's own error logs confirm the warning, so waiting simply lets a predictable outage happen.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because backups protect the data. But a restore means downtime and losing changes since the last copy, which a planned switch avoids.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the IT manager owns the runbook. But the runbook already assigns this switch to the administrator on a confirmed warning, so asking again only spends the time.

tips: Eliminate: A doubts a warning the logs confirm, and B accepts an outage and data loss that early warning lets the team avoid.
Final two: D beats C because the runbook already gives the administrator the switch on a confirmed warning; asking again wastes the lead time.
Exam cue: when early detection gives a confirmed warning and procedure assigns the response, use the lead time to act in a planned way.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR-03 (mechanisms are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-03 (hardware is maintained, replaced, and removed commensurate with risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Artificial intelligence (AI) assisted detection spots trouble early; for resilience, it must catch events before they disrupt the business' (notes 2.2.9 AI-Assisted Detection and Resilience). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Word-tell sweep, 18 Nov 2026: option B reworded.

questions.question: A pottery studio's quarterly security report to leaders shows every metric green, but its online shop, launched last month, has no security metrics yet. What should the security manager add as BEST?

options.A: Nothing more, as every metric in this quarter's report is green
options.B: A note that the new shop's risks are not yet measured
options.C: The full technical dashboard behind every metric
options.D: The passing result of the shop's pre-launch security test

questions.key_concept: Reports show only what is measured; new or unmeasured areas are stated plainly so an all-green view does not mislead leaders.
questions.pre_read: Think about what a green report can and cannot tell leaders.
questions.correct_explanation: Green covers only what is measured. A report that shows every metric green while a new online shop has no metrics leaves leaders believing all risk is covered, so the manager states plainly that the shop is not yet measured. The pre-launch test result is the runner-up: it shows the shop was checked once, but a single past test is not ongoing measurement and still hides the gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because nothing is red. But green covers only what is measured, and the new shop has no measures at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more detail seems more open. But leaders need the gap stated plainly, not a technical dashboard that buries it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it shows the shop was checked. But one past test is not ongoing measurement, and leaders would still miss that the shop is unmeasured.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an all-green report as complete, and C buries the point in technical detail leaders cannot use.
Final two: B beats D because a single past test leaves the shop unmeasured; the report must say plainly what it does not cover.
Exam cue: an all-green report covers only what is measured; tell leaders about new or unmeasured areas.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.1 (Measures Documentation: scope distinguishes the total risk from the risks currently being measured); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.2 (Measurement Reporting: reports give context, such as the risk indicated and what action or decision may be needed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Green covers only what is measured; reports still need new risks, unmeasured areas and trends heading toward a limit' (notes 2.4.5 Dashboards, Scorecards and Reports). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2.3 Security awareness. AI-boosted phishing and deepfakes
questions.question: Two members tell a gym chain's front-desk clerk they got fluent, personal texts, likely AI-written, from a fake 'membership team' urging them to renew through a link. What should the clerk do FIRST?

options.A: Note the texts in the front desk log and carry on
options.B: Pass the texts' details to the security team
options.C: Warn all members on the gym's social media page
options.D: Reply to the sender's number asking them to stop

questions.key_concept: Scams that use the organization's name, including fluent AI-written texts to customers, go to the security team, which confirms them and decides the response.
questions.pre_read: Recall what staff should do with signs of a scam aimed at anyone linked to the organization.
questions.correct_explanation: Scams aimed at customers are security events too, and fluent AI-written texts can reach every member at once. Passing the details to the security team lets it confirm the scam, have the link blocked and decide how members are warned. A public warning is the runner-up: members may need one, but the clerk would be speaking for the gym on a channel they do not own, before anyone has confirmed the facts.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it records what members said. But a desk log is not a report; the security team never sees it, and other members stay exposed.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: members may need a warning. But the security team must first confirm the scam and decide the response; the gym's public channels are not the clerk's.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it seems to confront the scammer. But replying confirms the number reaches a real person and protects no other member.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps the report in a desk log nobody acts on, and D engages the scammer, which protects no one.
Final two: B beats C because the security team confirms the scam and decides the warning; a public post from the desk is outside the clerk's role.
Exam cue: when you learn of a scam using your organization's name, report it to the security team first; they decide who warns whom.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2(3) (Literacy Training and Awareness | Social Engineering and Mining); NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) Section 2.8 (Information Integrity: deepfakes and content that impersonates others)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Generative AI writes fluent, personalized lures in many languages, at scale' (notes 2.3.5 AI-Boosted Phishing and Deepfakes). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 2.2 Redundancy. Testing BC and DR plans
questions.question: An organ builder replaced its order system with new vendor software, and the operations manager says the old-system recovery plan needs updating before the tabletop. Which reply from the continuity coordinator is BEST?

options.A: Agree; and test the updated plan at the tabletop exercise
options.B: Disagree; the tabletop will reveal what the new system changed
options.C: Disagree; the new vendor's support now handles recovery
options.D: Agree; and test the updated plan in a full interruption test

questions.key_concept: Recovery plans are updated after every major change, such as replacing a system, and then tested in their new form.
questions.pre_read: Recall when a recovery plan should be reviewed and updated.
questions.correct_explanation: A plan must reflect the system as it is now, and a major change such as replacing the system triggers a review and update; testing then checks the new plan. Letting the tabletop find the changes is the runner-up: tests do expose gaps, but walking through steps for a system no longer in use spends the exercise on a gap everyone already knows.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: tests do expose gaps. But this gap is already known, so the tabletop would rehearse steps for a system that is no longer in use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor supports its software. But support helps fix the product; the organ builder still owns its data, settings and recovery plan.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it is the most realistic test. But a full interruption is the riskiest test, needs senior management approval and does not suit a freshly rewritten plan.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes the vendor owns the organ builder's recovery, and D jumps to the riskiest test with a freshly rewritten plan.
Final two: A beats B because a known change goes into the plan first; a test should check the current plan, not rediscover a known gap.
Exam cue: update the plan after every major change, real event and test, then test the updated plan.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.6 (Plan Maintenance: the plan is reviewed whenever significant changes occur to any element of it); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-2 (Contingency Plan)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Update the plan after every test, real event and major change; senior management approves disruptive tests' (notes 2.2.7 Testing and Maintaining BC and DR Plans). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): candle maker became an organ builder (setting overuse); D also names the updated plan, so the stem's 'needs updating' is not echoed only in the key. Key no longer the lone shortest option.

questions.subtopic: 2.4 Measuring effectiveness. Using measurement to improve
questions.question: A stationery wholesaler's quarterly metrics review finds three red items, and the team agrees on each one's cause. Which next step should the security manager take as BEST?

options.A: Give each fix one named owner and a firm due date
options.B: Add weekly metrics for each red area, each with a named tracker
options.C: Lower the three targets and let the items turn amber
options.D: Retire the three metrics that keep showing red

questions.key_concept: Metrics drive improvement when each agreed fix has a named owner and a due date, followed by measuring again.
questions.pre_read: Think about what turns a red metric into a change in the outcome.
questions.correct_explanation: Measurement improves security only when it leads to action. Giving each fix a named owner and a due date turns the agreed causes into tracked work, and the next measurement shows whether it worked. More metrics is the runner-up: closer watching can feel like progress, but extra measures without owners only describe the problem more often.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: closer watching gives faster feedback. But without an owner and a due date, more measures describe the problem more often without fixing it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because amber looks better. But lowering targets changes the number, not the outcome, and hides the gap from leaders.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the metrics are uncomfortable. But they are doing their job; retiring them hides problems the team has just agreed are real.

tips: Eliminate: C changes the target instead of the outcome, and D removes the metrics exactly when they are showing real problems.
Final two: A beats B because a fix happens when someone owns it by a date; more metrics only watch the problem.
Exam cue: turn each finding into a fix with one owner and a due date, then measure again to confirm it worked.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PM-6 (Measures of Performance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Give each fix an owner and a due date, then measure again to confirm it worked' (notes 2.4.6 Using Measurement to Improve). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): B carries 'named' too (bank-wide word tell); C loses 'so' and gains 'and'; the key is no longer the lone shortest option.

questions.question: A dog grooming chain is setting rules for staff use of chatbots and image generators. Which NIST publication should the security manager propose to leaders as the BEST structure for this work?

options.A: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
options.B: NIST AI 100-2 adversarial machine learning taxonomy
options.C: NIST SP 800-63B-4 authentication guidelines
options.D: NIST AI 100-1 AI Risk Management Framework

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework structures how an organization governs, maps, measures and manages the risks of AI.
questions.pre_read: Recall which NIST publication covers which kind of risk.
questions.correct_explanation: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) is built for AI risk: its Govern, Map, Measure and Manage functions cover issues such as unreliable or biased outputs and accountability for AI use, which general security frameworks do not comprehensively address. CSF 2.0 is the runner-up: it is strong for cybersecurity governance and can sit alongside, but it is not built around AI-specific risks.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: CSF 2.0 has a Govern function. But it is built for cybersecurity risk in general and does not comprehensively address AI-specific risks such as biased outputs.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is a NIST AI publication. But it names attacks on AI systems and their mitigations; it is a taxonomy, not a framework for managing AI risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI tools need sign-in controls. But it sets digital identity and authentication rules, not a structure for managing AI risk.

tips: Eliminate: B catalogs attacks on AI rather than structuring how AI risk is managed, and C covers digital identity.
Final two: D beats A because the AI RMF is built for AI-specific risks such as biased outputs; CSF 2.0 covers cybersecurity in general.
Exam cue: match the publication to the job: CSF for cybersecurity programs, the AI RMF for managing AI risk, AI 100-2 for naming attacks on AI.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) Section 5 (AI RMF Core: the GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE functions organize AI risk management); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) Appendix B (How AI Risks Differ from Traditional Software Risks: AI systems bring risks that current risk frameworks do not comprehensively address)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) AI Risk Management Framework can structure this work' (notes 2.1.8 Governing AI Use). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 7, 12 Nov 2026. Batch 7 final fix round (12 Nov 2026): the security manager now proposes and leaders choose (matches cc_d1_206 and notes 1.3); D carries its document number like A to C; C no longer uses the series title.

questions.question: A five-person tile shop's RACI chart for its yearly website certificate renewal marks the office manager both Responsible and Accountable. How should the IT coordinator BEST treat this entry?

options.A: Keep it; it meets RACI's one-Accountable rule
options.B: Split it; it breaks RACI's separate-roles rule
options.C: Add the shop's owner as a second Accountable person
options.D: Mark the office manager Consulted, not Responsible

questions.key_concept: One person can be both Responsible and Accountable; RACI requires exactly one Accountable person per task, not different people for the two roles.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each letter in a RACI chart means for one task.
questions.correct_explanation: RACI requires exactly one Accountable person per task. It does not require the doer and the answerer to be different people, and in a small team one person often holds both, so this entry meets the rule. Splitting the roles is the runner-up: it sounds like extra control, but RACI has no separate-roles rule. Separating duties is a different control, kept for high-risk tasks such as payments.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: separating roles can add oversight. But RACI has no separate-roles rule; its rule is one Accountable person per task, and that person may also do the work.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the owner runs the shop. But two Accountable people for one task leaves each assuming the other will act.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because input is part of the task. But Consulted means advising before the work, and the office manager does the renewal.

tips: Eliminate: C gives one task two Accountable people, and D labels the person who does the work as only giving input.
Final two: A beats B because RACI needs exactly one Accountable person, not two different people for R and A; small teams often combine them.
Exam cue: RACI's hard rule is one A per task; R and A may sit with the same person.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'In a small team one person can be both Responsible and Accountable for a task' (notes 2.1.3 GRC Accountability: RACI and Reporting Lines). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026. Batch 8 final fix round (18 Nov 2026): key concept no longer says one Accountable person is RACI's only rule.

questions.question: A coding academy's contract allows only its approved AI tool; for this term's proof, the security analyst exported just the last week of gateway logs, though a year is kept. Which step is BEST?

options.A: Send last week's logs, noting the rest was normal
options.B: Send the AI use policy and the term's staff training records
options.C: Send logs that cover every week of the term instead
options.D: Send the AI tool vendor's latest security certificate

questions.key_concept: Compliance evidence must cover the whole period an obligation applies to; a sample from part of it cannot prove the rest.
questions.pre_read: Recall what makes compliance evidence convincing.
questions.correct_explanation: The contract applies all term, so the proof must cover all term. The gateway still holds a year of logs, so the analyst pulls and sends the full period. Sending the last week with a note is the runner-up: it is real operating evidence, but it says nothing about the other weeks, and the note only claims they were similar.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: logs do show the control operating. But one week cannot prove the rest of the term, and a note is a claim, not evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because policy and training are required. But they show the rule was set and taught, not that staff followed it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor runs the approved tool. But its certificate covers the vendor's controls, not which AI services staff used.

tips: Eliminate: B shows the rule exists and was taught, not that it was followed, and D covers the vendor, not staff use.
Final two: C beats A because evidence must span the whole period the contract covers; one week plus a note leaves most of the term unproven.
Exam cue: check that the evidence covers the full period and scope of the obligation, not just the part that is easy to pull.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed); NIST CSF 2.0 DE.CM-03 (personnel activity and technology usage are monitored to find potentially adverse events)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Collect evidence as work happens, such as logs, tickets and test results' (notes 2.1.4 Compliance Obligations and Evidence). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A cut-flower grower's continuity coordinator finished a business impact analysis (BIA) ranking every function's recovery order, and the IT manager offers to sign it off. What is the coordinator's BEST next step?

options.A: Accept the IT manager's sign-off and begin recovery planning
options.B: Ask each function owner to approve their own ratings instead
options.C: Submit the BIA results to senior management for approval
options.D: Choose recovery sites now and seek approval afterward

questions.key_concept: Senior management approves BIA results, because ranking functions for recovery sets priorities for the whole organization.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a business impact analysis produces and how its results are used.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA that ranks the recovery order of every function sets priorities across the whole business, so senior management approves its results before recovery strategies are chosen. Function owners rate harm in their own areas, but none of them can settle trade-offs between functions. That is why their separate approvals, the runner-up, are not enough: approval must come from the level that answers for the whole organization.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because IT will run much of the recovery. But the IT manager speaks for one function and cannot set priorities for the whole business.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: function owners rated the harm in their own areas. But separate approvals of their own ratings leave no one to settle the order across functions.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because sites take time to arrange. But sites are matched to approved recovery targets; choosing first risks paying for the wrong ones.

tips: Eliminate: A gives one function's manager a whole-business decision, and D picks sites before the targets they must meet are approved.
Final two: C beats B because ranking functions against each other is a business-wide trade-off that only senior management can settle; owners speak for their own areas.
Exam cue: when a result sets priorities across the whole organization, approval belongs to senior management, not to any one department.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2 (Conduct the Business Impact Analysis (BIA): BIA results feed strategy development for the BCP and DRP); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Set each function's maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) and recovery targets, then rank functions; senior management approves the results' (notes 2.2.3 Business Impact Analysis (BIA)). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A bike retailer's recovery plan, owned by the IT manager, has the system administrator hold the warm site to the main site's baseline, but its servers lack endpoint protection. What should the administrator do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the IT manager to accept the baseline gap for now
options.B: Treat the warm site as safe while it stays idle
options.C: Install endpoint protection to match the main-site baseline
options.D: Propose a hot site whose provider supplies endpoint protection

questions.key_concept: A recovery site needs security controls equivalent to the main site's, in place before it is ever used.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a recovery site must have besides equipment and data.
questions.correct_explanation: A recovery site needs controls equivalent to the main site's, because it will run real work and data the moment it is used. The plan assigns this task to the administrator, so installing endpoint protection to the baseline is in-role and comes first. Asking the IT manager to accept the gap is the runner-up: escalation suits decisions outside one's authority, but this fix is already assigned.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the IT manager owns the plan. But the plan assigns this fix to the administrator; acceptance with a review date is for risks deliberately kept, not assigned work.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because an idle site holds no live work. But a disaster can strike at any time, and the site must be secure from its first minute of use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because hot sites are the readiest. But readiness is about recovery speed; the missing control is a gap the administrator can close at the warm site.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves a site unprotected that must run securely the moment it is used, and D pays for a faster site to fix one missing control.
Final two: C beats A because the plan assigns this fix to the administrator; asking for acceptance hands back work that is already theirs.
Exam cue: a recovery site gets the same security controls as the main site, and when a procedure assigns the fix to you, you carry it out.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-7 (Alternate Processing Site); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.4.3 (Alternate Sites)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Give the recovery site the same security controls as the main site, including monitoring, from the moment it runs' (notes 2.2.6 Recovery Sites). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A plant nursery chain's IT manager says its new AI threat-monitoring tool must not run on the server cluster it watches, though that would cost less. How should the security analyst BEST respond?

options.A: Disagree; the tool spots threats faster beside the cluster
options.B: Agree; a cluster outage would also take down the monitoring
options.C: Agree; separate hosting makes the tool's alerts more accurate
options.D: Disagree; its alerts already reach analysts' phones off-site

questions.key_concept: Detection should run where a failure of the monitored systems cannot also take it down, so it keeps working during the outage.
questions.pre_read: Recall how monitoring supports resilience during an outage.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring that shares the cluster it watches fails in the same outage, leaving the team blind just when attackers can exploit the confusion. Separate hosting keeps detection working through the event it warns about, so the IT manager is right. Sending alerts to analysts' phones off-site is the runner-up: the alerts travel elsewhere, but the tool that raises them would still stop in the outage.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because nearby tools seem quicker. But alert speed hardly depends on where the tool runs; the real issue is that one failure would stop both.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it agrees with the IT manager. But hosting does not change how accurate detections are; the reason is surviving a cluster outage.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the alerts do leave the cluster. But the tool that raises them runs on the cluster, so an outage stops the alerts at their source.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a speed gain that location barely gives, and C credits separate hosting with an accuracy gain it does not bring.
Final two: B beats D because the tool itself must keep running through the outage; sending alerts off-site does not help once the tool has stopped.
Exam cue: ask whether a safeguard survives the failure it is meant to catch; a monitor on the platform it watches does not.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR-03 (mechanisms are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Run monitoring where a main-site failure cannot take it down, and restore it early' (notes 2.2.9 AI-Assisted Detection and Resilience). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026.

questions.question: A moving company's executives praise security in newsletters but have rejected every awareness plan needing staff time or money for two years; staff call security just talk. What should the awareness lead propose as BEST?

options.A: Leaders writing more security articles for the newsletter
options.B: Leaders giving the program the resources it needs
options.C: A required yearly course with completion rates by team
options.D: Monthly rankings of teams by phishing clicks

questions.key_concept: Leaders shape security culture through their actions, including funding the program, not only through their words.
questions.pre_read: Recall how leaders set the tone for security culture.
questions.correct_explanation: Culture follows what leaders do, not only what they say: praising security while turning down every plan to act on it tells staff it does not matter. Giving the program the resources it needs shows the praise is meant. A required course tracked by completion rates is the runner-up: it builds skills, but it cannot fix a message from the top, and completing a course does not prove changed behavior.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it keeps leaders' voices visible. But staff already hear the praise; more words without resources deepen the sense that it is just talk.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: required training builds skills, and completion rates are easy to track. But staff would still see leaders refusing to back the work, so the culture problem stays.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because rankings create pressure. But public shaming makes people hide mistakes, which weakens the reporting a healthy culture depends on.

tips: Eliminate: A adds more of the talk staff already discount, and D uses shaming that drives mistakes into hiding.
Final two: B beats C because culture follows leaders' actions, including funding; a required course trains staff without changing what leaders signal.
Exam cue: when staff doubt that leaders mean it, look for the option where leaders act, by following the rules or by funding the work.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving); NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 Section 1.6.1 (Head of Organization: the program is well-supported by resources, including personnel and funding)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Leaders set the tone: they follow the same rules, talk about security and fund it' (notes 2.3.1 Security Culture and Leadership). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026. Batch 8 final fix round (18 Nov 2026): stem restores what leaders withheld (staff time or money), so the key no longer rests on an inference. Option D shortened so the key is not the lone shortest option.

questions.question: An orchard cooperative is moving staff from personal AI accounts to its approved assistant in uneven waves over ten months; it tracks the share moved. Which addition BEST shows early if it is on pace?

options.A: Monthly reports of the share moved to date
options.B: A monthly count of prompts sent to the assistant
options.C: A list of the personal AI tools that staff have tried
options.D: A quarterly interim target ahead of the final goal

questions.key_concept: Metrics for long efforts use interim targets as well as the final one, so progress can be judged along the way.
questions.pre_read: Recall what turns a raw measure into a metric that tracks progress.
questions.correct_explanation: A metric tracks progress against a target, and a long effort needs interim targets. Because teams move in uneven waves, a straight line to 100% says little; quarterly targets set from the wave plan show whether the move is on pace in time to act. Monthly reports of the share moved are the runner-up: they arrive sooner, but with no interim target, 20% in month three cannot show the pace.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: monthly figures arrive sooner. But a share alone is a measure; with uneven waves and no interim target to compare it with, no one can tell the pace.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it shows the assistant is used. But prompt volume is activity, not the share of staff who have left personal accounts.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it shows what staff use. But an inventory is a list, not a measure judged against any target.

tips: Eliminate: B counts activity rather than the share of staff who have moved, and C is an inventory with no target to judge progress against.
Final two: D beats A because an interim target says where the share should be by each point; more frequent figures without one cannot show whether the move is on pace.
Exam cue: for goals that take months, pair the final target with interim ones, so the metric warns early.

questions.question: A dance school chain's backup KPI met its 99% on-schedule target, but its KRI, systems with no restore test in a year, rose from 3 to 11. Which conclusion is BEST?

options.A: Backups met their target, which means recovery risk stays low
options.B: The KRI rose because the 99% target was set too low
options.C: Backups ran on time, but the untested systems now exceed tolerance
options.D: The backups ran on time, but more systems lack proven recovery

questions.key_concept: A KPI can meet its target while a KRI shows a risk growing, because they measure performance and exposure separately.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a KPI and a KRI each measure.
questions.correct_explanation: A key performance indicator (KPI) and a key risk indicator (KRI) answer different questions. The backup KPI shows the jobs ran on schedule, while the KRI shows more systems whose recovery is unproven. Both readings are true at once. Concluding that a green KPI means recovery risk stays low is the runner-up and the classic trap: performance can look fine while risk grows.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the KPI is green. But a met KPI shows the process ran, not that recovery risk stays low; the KRI shows untested systems almost quadrupled.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a stricter target sounds safer. But the KPI counts backup jobs run on schedule; raising it tests no restores, so the untested systems would still grow.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the KRI nearly quadrupled. But no threshold is given; a KRI warns as exposure nears a tolerance limit, and a rise alone does not show it passed.

tips: Eliminate: B blames the KRI's rise on the KPI target, though more on-time jobs test no restores, and C declares tolerance passed with no threshold given; a rising KRI is a warning.
Final two: D beats A because a met KPI says backups ran, not that recovery is proven; the KRI shows more systems lack a restore test.
Exam cue: read a KPI as 'are we performing?' and a KRI as 'is risk growing?'; both answers can be true at once.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 2.4 (Metrics: key risk indicators and key performance indicators)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'KPIs show performance; KRIs warn of risk' (notes 2.4.3 Key Performance and Key Risk Indicators). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026. Batch 8 final fix round (18 Nov 2026): C no longer contradicts the stem's met target (now a real misconception: a rising KRI read as a passed tolerance), and the key now states the insight (recovery unproven for more systems) instead of restating the stem.

questions.question: A car-wash chain's operations team wants its live security dashboard, which names each site's unpatched systems, on a waiting-room screen to reassure customers. What should the security analyst propose as BEST?

options.A: Show the full dashboard as is and let openness build trust
options.B: Show it with a notice that fixes are under way
options.C: Show staff the full view and customers their own site's list
options.D: Show staff the full view and customers a summary

questions.key_concept: Match a metrics view to its audience: detail that helps attackers stays with the staff who act on it; the public gets a summary.
questions.pre_read: Recall how a metrics view is matched to its audience.
questions.correct_explanation: A dashboard naming unpatched systems is built for the staff who fix them; on a public screen it tells attackers where to look. Showing staff the full view and customers a plain summary serves both audiences. Showing customers only the systems at their own site is the runner-up: it trims the view, but it still names that site's unpatched systems to the people standing in it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because openness can build trust. But publishing the systems you have not patched hands attackers a target list.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a notice could reassure customers, the team's goal. But the screen would still list the unpatched systems, and the notice tells attackers they are not fixed yet.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it trims the view to one site. But it still names that site's unpatched systems to the people standing in it, which is the detail an attacker wants.

tips: Eliminate: A publishes a target list, and B adds a reassuring notice while still listing the weak systems.
Final two: D beats C because trimming the view to one site still names its weak systems to the people standing there; detail that helps attackers stays with the staff who fix it.
Exam cue: choose the format and the detail for the audience; information that helps attackers never goes on a public display.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-22 (Publicly Accessible Content)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Know the audience first: the board, senior management, risk owners or technical teams' (notes 2.4.5 Dashboards, Scorecards and Reports). Original scenario and wording; no prep-bank, CBK or certification-body training text used. CC D2 batch 8, 13 Nov 2026. Batch 8 final fix round (18 Nov 2026): runner-up C no longer states its own flaw and now shares 'customers' with the key; A gains an 'and' so only the key does not join two parts.

questions.question: A community sports center will move member bookings to a new cloud system next month, but front-desk staff's role-based training still covers the old one. What is the awareness lead's BEST action?

options.A: Update their training before the system goes live
options.B: Add the new system to next year's refresher
options.C: Send all staff a general security reminder
options.D: Give staff the vendor's user guide and a login

questions.key_concept: Role-based training is updated when a system changes, before staff start using it, not at the next scheduled refresh.
questions.pre_read: Recall what role-based training covers and for whom.
questions.correct_explanation: Role-based training must keep pace with the systems a role uses, so a new booking system calls for updated training before staff work in it. Waiting for next year's refresher is the runner-up: the topic would be covered eventually, but staff would handle member data in the new system for months without its security steps.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the refresher will cover it eventually. But staff would use the new system for months without knowing its security steps.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reminders are cheap. But a general message for everyone does not teach the job steps of a new system.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors document their product. But a user guide teaches features, not the center's own rules for handling member data.

tips: Eliminate: C gives everyone a general message instead of role skills, and D swaps training for a product manual.
Final two: A beats B because role-based training changes when the system does; waiting a year leaves staff untrained on a system they use every day.
Exam cue: a new system, role or duty triggers role-based training before the work starts, not at the next scheduled cycle.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-3 (Role-based Training); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AT-02 (individuals in specialized roles are provided with awareness and training to perform relevant tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Role-based training is also updated when a system a role uses changes, before staff work in it' (notes 2.3.2 Awareness, Training and Education).
